subject: Accountancy
title: Capital Expenditure vs Revenue Expenditure
formulaOrRule: Capital Expenditure: benefits extend beyond one year (acquisition or improvement of fixed assets). Revenue Expenditure: benefits exhausted within the year (day-to-day operating expenses).

variablesOrTerms.Capital Expenditure: Shown in Balance Sheet as addition to assets
variablesOrTerms.Revenue Expenditure: Debited to Trading or Profit & Loss Account

derivationOrExplanation: Correct distinction is vital for true profit calculation and asset valuation. Capital expenditure is not charged fully against current revenue; only depreciation is. Revenue expenditure is matched against current period revenue. Misclassification (e.g., treating a capital item as revenue) understates profit and assets, and vice versa. Deferred revenue expenditure is a hybrid that is written off over several years.

flashcard.front: How is capital expenditure treated differently from revenue expenditure in the final accounts?
flashcard.back: Capital expenditure is capitalised (shown as asset) and only depreciated; revenue expenditure is fully charged to the Profit & Loss Account in the year it is incurred.

subject: Accountancy
title: Fundamental Accounting Equation
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Capital}$$

variablesOrTerms.Assets: Resources owned by the business (cash, inventory, fixed assets)
variablesOrTerms.Liabilities: Obligations or amounts owed to outsiders
variablesOrTerms.Capital: Owner's equity or claim on the assets

derivationOrExplanation: The equation is based on the dual aspect concept: every transaction has two aspects. When assets increase, either liabilities or capital must increase by the same amount (or another asset decreases). Rearrangement gives Capital = Assets − Liabilities. All journal entries and the balance sheet are built on this identity.

flashcard.front: State the fundamental accounting equation and rearrange it to find Capital.
flashcard.back: Assets = Liabilities + Capital; therefore Capital = Assets − Liabilities.
flashcard.hint: Think dual aspect / balance sheet identity.

subject: Accountancy
title: Accounting for Dishonour of a Bill
formulaOrRule: In drawer’s books on dishonour: Debit Drawee’s A/c, Credit Bills Receivable A/c (and Credit Bank if discounted or endorsed). Noting charges are also debited to Drawee’s A/c.

variablesOrTerms.Dishonour: Acceptor fails to pay on the due date
variablesOrTerms.Noting: Official recording of dishonour by a Notary Public
variablesOrTerms.Noting Charges: Fee paid to the Notary, recoverable from the drawee

derivationOrExplanation: When a bill is dishonoured the original credit given to the drawee is reversed and the debt is restored. If the bill had been discounted, the bank recovers the amount from the drawer, so the drawer debits the drawee and credits the bank. Noting charges paid by the holder are added to the amount recoverable from the drawee. A new bill may be drawn for the total amount including interest and noting charges.

flashcard.front: What entry is passed in the drawer’s books when a bill retained by him is dishonoured?
flashcard.back: Drawee’s A/c Dr. To Bills Receivable A/c (and To Cash/Bank for noting charges if paid).

subject: Accountancy
title: Key Terms and Parties in a Bill of Exchange
formulaOrRule: Drawer (maker) draws the bill on Drawee (acceptor). Payee is the person who receives payment. Due date = Date of bill + Tenure + 3 days of grace (in India).

variablesOrTerms.Payee: Person entitled to receive the amount
variablesOrTerms.Days of Grace: 3 extra days allowed by law in India

derivationOrExplanation: A bill of exchange is an unconditional order in writing. After acceptance it becomes a legal instrument. Discounting, endorsement and retirement are common transactions. Noting and protesting are required if the bill is dishonoured. Accounting entries differ for drawer and drawee.

flashcard.front: Who are the three parties to a bill of exchange and what is the due date rule in India?
flashcard.back: Drawer, Drawee, Payee. Due date = Date + Tenure + 3 days of grace.

subject: Accountancy
title: Journal Entries for Depreciation
formulaOrRule: When Provision for Depreciation A/c is maintained: Debit Depreciation A/c, Credit Provision for Depreciation A/c. At year-end: Debit P&L A/c, Credit Depreciation A/c. Asset appears at original cost; provision is shown as deduction.

variablesOrTerms.Direct method: Depreciation directly credited to Asset A/c (less common in exam presentation)

derivationOrExplanation: Two methods exist: (1) Direct – depreciation is credited to the Asset Account itself so the asset appears at written-down value. (2) Indirect (Provision) – Asset remains at historical cost and a separate Provision for Depreciation Account accumulates the charge. The second method is preferred for disclosure and is commonly examined. On sale of asset the provision is transferred to the Asset Account before calculating profit or loss.

flashcard.front: Pass the journal entry for charging depreciation when a Provision for Depreciation Account is maintained.
flashcard.back: Depreciation A/c Dr. To Provision for Depreciation A/c; then Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Depreciation A/c.

subject: Accountancy
title: Straight Line Method (SLM) of Depreciation
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Annual Depreciation} = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Scrap Value}}{\text{Useful Life}}$$

variablesOrTerms.Scrap Value: Estimated residual value at end of useful life
variablesOrTerms.Useful Life: Expected number of years the asset will be used

derivationOrExplanation: SLM assumes the asset loses equal value each year. Total depreciable amount is Cost − Scrap. Dividing by estimated life yields a constant annual charge. Rate of depreciation = (Annual Depreciation / Cost) × 100. The method is simple and produces a straight-line decline in book value.

flashcard.front: Write the formula for annual depreciation under the Straight Line Method.
flashcard.back: (Cost − Scrap Value) / Useful Life

Active Recall: Q: Write the formula for annual depreciation under the Straight Line Method. | A: (Cost − Scrap Value) / Useful Life

subject: Accountancy
title: Written Down Value (WDV) Method
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Depreciation} = \text{Book Value at beginning of year} \times \text{Rate}\%$$

variablesOrTerms.Rate: Fixed percentage applied each year on the diminishing balance

derivationOrExplanation: Under WDV (reducing balance) method, depreciation is charged at a constant rate on the written-down value. Consequently the absolute amount of depreciation decreases every year. This method is preferred for assets that lose more value in early years (e.g., vehicles, computers). Formula for rate when scrap value and life are known: Rate = $1 - \sqrt[n]{\frac{\text{Scrap}}{\text{Cost}}}$.

flashcard.front: How is annual depreciation calculated under the Written Down Value method?
flashcard.back: Book Value at the beginning of the year × fixed rate %.

subject: Accountancy
title: Key Adjustments in Final Accounts
formulaOrRule: Closing Stock appears in Trading A/c (credit) and Balance Sheet (asset). Outstanding expenses: add to expense in P&L and show as liability. Prepaid expenses: deduct from expense and show as asset. Depreciation: debit P&L, deduct from asset.

variablesOrTerms.Trading A/c: Gross Profit calculation (Sales − Cost of Goods Sold)
variablesOrTerms.Profit & Loss A/c: Net Profit calculation after operating and non-operating items

derivationOrExplanation: Adjustments ensure matching principle and accrual basis. Closing stock is valued at cost or NRV whichever is lower. Outstanding/prepaid items adjust the expense to the correct accounting period. Depreciation allocates cost of fixed assets. All adjustments have dual effect (one in final accounts, one in Balance Sheet).

flashcard.front: Where does Closing Stock appear in the final accounts?
flashcard.back: Credit side of Trading Account and under Current Assets in the Balance Sheet.

subject: Accountancy
title: Classification of Assets in the Balance Sheet
formulaOrRule: Non-current Assets: Fixed Assets (Tangible & Intangible), Non-current Investments, Long-term Loans & Advances. Current Assets: Current Investments, Inventories, Trade Receivables, Cash & Cash Equivalents, Short-term Loans & Advances.

variablesOrTerms.Tangible Assets: Physical assets (land, building, plant, machinery, furniture)

derivationOrExplanation: Assets are classified according to the period within which they are expected to be realised or consumed. Non-current assets provide long-term benefits. Current assets are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within the normal operating cycle or twelve months. Correct classification is essential for calculating liquidity and solvency ratios and for presenting a true and fair view.

flashcard.front: Give two examples each of tangible and intangible fixed assets.
flashcard.back: Tangible: Building, Machinery. Intangible: Goodwill, Patents (or Trademarks, Copyrights).

subject: Accountancy
title: Closing Entries for Trading and P&L Accounts
formulaOrRule: All nominal accounts (expenses & incomes) are closed by transferring their balances to Trading or Profit & Loss Account. Gross Profit is transferred to P&L; Net Profit is transferred to Capital Account.

variablesOrTerms.Closing Entry: Journal entry that transfers the balance of a temporary account to a permanent account
variablesOrTerms.Nominal Accounts: Accounts of expenses, losses, incomes and gains

derivationOrExplanation: At the end of the accounting period, temporary (nominal) accounts are closed so that they start with zero balance in the next period. Expenses are debited to Trading/P&L and the expense accounts are credited. Incomes are credited to Trading/P&L and the income accounts are debited. The resulting Gross Profit or Net Profit is finally transferred to the Capital Account, which is a permanent account.

flashcard.front: What is the purpose of closing entries?
flashcard.back: To transfer the balances of all temporary (nominal) accounts to Trading or Profit & Loss Account so that these accounts start afresh in the next accounting period.

subject: Accountancy
title: Items Appearing in Trading Account
formulaOrRule: Debit side: Opening Stock, Net Purchases, Direct Expenses (wages, carriage inward, freight, fuel, royalty, etc.). Credit side: Net Sales, Closing Stock. Balancing figure = Gross Profit (or Gross Loss).

variablesOrTerms.Direct Expenses: Expenses directly related to production or purchase of goods

derivationOrExplanation: The Trading Account matches the cost of goods sold against sales revenue to ascertain Gross Profit. Only direct costs are charged here. Indirect expenses (office salaries, rent, advertising, depreciation of office assets, etc.) go to the Profit & Loss Account. Correct classification between direct and indirect is essential for accurate Gross Profit.

flashcard.front: Name any four items that appear on the debit side of the Trading Account.
flashcard.back: Opening Stock, Purchases, Wages, Carriage Inwards (or Freight, Fuel, Royalty, etc.).

subject: Accountancy
title: Sequence of Preparing Final Accounts
formulaOrRule: 1. Trial Balance 2. Adjustments 3. Adjusted Trial Balance (optional) 4. Trading Account 5. Profit & Loss Account 6. Balance Sheet.

variablesOrTerms.Adjustments: Outstanding, prepaid, depreciation, closing stock, provision for doubtful debts, etc.
variablesOrTerms.Adjusted Trial Balance: Trial Balance after incorporating all adjustments

derivationOrExplanation: The logical sequence ensures that all information is systematically processed. Adjustments are first recorded so that the Trading and Profit & Loss Accounts reflect the correct periodic figures. Gross Profit from the Trading Account is carried to the Profit & Loss Account. Net Profit (or Loss) is transferred to the Capital Account, which then appears in the Balance Sheet along with all assets and liabilities.

flashcard.front: List the correct sequence of preparing final accounts starting from the Trial Balance.
flashcard.back: Trial Balance → Adjustments → Trading Account → Profit & Loss Account → Balance Sheet.
flashcard.hint: From list of balances to statements.

subject: Accountancy
title: Rules of Debit and Credit (Traditional Approach)
formulaOrRule: Personal A/c: Debit the receiver, Credit the giver. Real A/c: Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out. Nominal A/c: Debit all expenses & losses, Credit all incomes & gains.

variablesOrTerms.Nominal A/c: Accounts of expenses, losses, incomes, gains

derivationOrExplanation: These golden rules are derived from the dual-aspect concept. Every transaction affects two accounts. Classification into Personal, Real and Nominal determines which side is debited or credited. Modern approach uses Assets/Expenses (debit increase) and Liabilities/Capital/Incomes (credit increase).

flashcard.front: State the three traditional rules of debit and credit.
flashcard.back: Personal: Debit receiver, Credit giver. Real: Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out. Nominal: Debit expenses/losses, Credit incomes/gains.

subject: Accountancy
title: Provision for Doubtful Debts – Accounting Treatment
formulaOrRule: New Provision required − Existing Provision = Amount debited (or credited) to Profit & Loss Account. Debtors are shown in Balance Sheet after deducting the closing provision.

variablesOrTerms.Provision for Doubtful Debts: Estimated loss on account of debts that may not be recovered

derivationOrExplanation: At year-end an estimate is made of debts that may prove bad. The difference between the required closing provision and the opening provision is adjusted through the Profit & Loss Account. Actual bad debts are first written off against the provision (or directly to P&L if no provision exists). The Balance Sheet shows debtors at net realisable value (Debtors − Provision).

flashcard.front: How is the amount charged to Profit & Loss Account for Provision for Doubtful Debts calculated?
flashcard.back: Closing Provision required minus Opening Provision (plus any further bad debts written off, depending on the method followed).

subject: Accountancy
title: Rectification through Suspense Account
formulaOrRule: One-sided errors are rectified by debiting or crediting the Suspense A/c to make the Trial Balance agree. Once the error is located, a correcting entry is passed that clears the Suspense A/c.

variablesOrTerms.Suspense A/c: Temporary account opened to balance the Trial Balance when it does not agree
variablesOrTerms.One-sided error: Error affecting only one account (e.g., omission of posting on one side)

derivationOrExplanation: When the Trial Balance fails to agree, the difference is placed in Suspense Account. After locating the error, the correct account is debited or credited and Suspense is closed. If all errors are found, Suspense balance becomes zero. Errors of principle and two-sided errors do not affect the Trial Balance and therefore do not go through Suspense.

flashcard.front: When is a Suspense Account used in rectification of errors?
flashcard.back: When the Trial Balance does not agree due to one-sided errors; the difference is temporarily placed in Suspense A/c until the errors are located and corrected.

subject: Accountancy
title: Types of Errors and Rectification
formulaOrRule: Errors of omission, commission, principle, and compensating errors. Errors affecting Trial Balance are rectified through Suspense A/c; others by journal entries.

variablesOrTerms.Compensating Error: Two or more errors that cancel each other’s effect on Trial Balance
variablesOrTerms.Suspense A/c: Temporary account to make Trial Balance agree

derivationOrExplanation: One-sided errors (affecting only one account) cause disagreement of Trial Balance and are routed through Suspense A/c. Two-sided errors are rectified by a proper journal entry that restores the correct debits and credits. After rectification, Suspense A/c should become zero if all errors are located.

flashcard.front: Which type of error does not affect the agreement of Trial Balance?
flashcard.back: Errors of principle and compensating errors (and complete omission of a transaction).

Two-sided errors are rectified by a proper journal entry that restores the correct debits and credits. After rectification, Suspense A/c should become zero if all errors are located.

subject: Accountancy
title: Errors Not Disclosed by Trial Balance
formulaOrRule: Errors of complete omission, errors of principle, compensating errors, and errors of recording a transaction on the correct sides but with wrong amounts that cancel out.

variablesOrTerms.Error of complete omission: Transaction completely left out of the books
variablesOrTerms.Error of principle: Wrong classification between capital and revenue items
variablesOrTerms.Compensating error: Two or more errors that neutralise each other’s effect on the Trial Balance

derivationOrExplanation: The Trial Balance only verifies arithmetic accuracy of postings. It cannot detect errors that keep the debit and credit totals equal. Awareness of these limitations prevents over-reliance on a balanced Trial Balance.

subject: Economics
title: Long-Run Average Cost Curve (LAC)
formulaOrRule: LAC is the envelope of a series of short-run Average Cost curves. It is typically U-shaped due to economies and diseconomies of scale.

variablesOrTerms.Economies of Scale: Fall in LAC as output expands
variablesOrTerms.Diseconomies of Scale: Rise in LAC beyond optimum scale

derivationOrExplanation: In the long run the firm can choose the optimal plant size for every output level. Each short-run AC curve corresponds to a fixed plant. The LAC curve touches each SAC curve at the lowest possible cost for that output. The falling portion of LAC reflects economies of scale; the rising portion reflects diseconomies. The minimum point of LAC is the long-run optimum scale of production.

flashcard.front: Why is the Long-Run Average Cost curve called an envelope curve?
flashcard.back: Because it is tangent to a family of short-run AC curves, showing the lowest possible average cost for each output level when plant size is variable.
flashcard.hint: Touches but does not cross SACs.

subject: Economics
title: Short-Run Cost Curves – Shapes and Relationships
formulaOrRule: TFC is horizontal; TVC and TC are inverse-S shaped. AFC falls continuously. AVC, AC and MC are U-shaped. MC cuts AVC and AC at their minimum points.

variablesOrTerms.AFC: Average Fixed Cost = TFC / Q (continuously declining)

derivationOrExplanation: Fixed costs do not change with output, so AFC declines as output rises (spreading overhead). Variable costs first increase at a decreasing rate (increasing returns) and later at an increasing rate (diminishing returns), producing the U-shape of AVC and MC. Because AC = AFC + AVC, AC is also U-shaped and lies above AVC. The MC curve intersects both AVC and AC at their lowest points – a necessary mathematical relationship.

flashcard.front: Why does the Average Fixed Cost curve continuously decline?
flashcard.back: Because total fixed cost remains constant while output increases, so fixed cost per unit keeps falling.

subject: Economics
title: Short-run Cost Relationships
formulaOrRule: $$\text{TC} = \text{TFC} + \text{TVC}$$; $$\text{AC} = \frac{\text{TC}}{Q}$$; $$\text{MC} = \frac{\Delta\text{TC}}{\Delta Q}$$; MC cuts AC and AVC at their minimum points.
derivationOrExplanation: Fixed costs do not change with output; variable costs do. MC is the additional cost of producing one more unit. Because MC first falls and then rises, AC and AVC are U-shaped. MC intersects both AC and AVC at their lowest points – a mathematical necessity when the marginal is below the average, the average falls, and vice versa.

flashcard.front: State the relationship between MC and AC.
flashcard.back: MC cuts AC at its minimum point. When MC < AC, AC falls; when MC > AC, AC rises.

subject: Economics
title: Total, Average and Marginal Revenue
formulaOrRule: $$\text{TR} = P \times Q$$\quad $$\text{AR} = \frac{\text{TR}}{Q} = P$$\quad $$\text{MR} = \frac{\Delta\text{TR}}{\Delta Q}$$

variablesOrTerms.AR: Average Revenue (equals price under uniform pricing)

derivationOrExplanation: Under perfect competition AR = MR = Price (horizontal demand curve). Under imperfect competition AR slopes downward and MR lies below AR. Relationship: when MR is positive TR rises, when MR is zero TR is maximum, when MR is negative TR falls. MR = AR − (change in AR caused by extra unit).

flashcard.front: What is the relationship between AR and MR under perfect competition?
flashcard.back: AR = MR = Price (both are horizontal lines).

subject: Economics
title: Cross Elasticity of Demand
formulaOrRule: $$e_c = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q_x}{\%\,\Delta P_y}$$
derivationOrExplanation: Cross elasticity measures how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good. For substitutes (tea and coffee) the coefficient is positive; for complements (car and petrol) it is negative. The magnitude indicates the strength of the relationship. Businesses use cross elasticity to predict the impact of competitors’ price changes and to design pricing strategies for related products.

flashcard.front: What does a positive cross elasticity of demand indicate?
flashcard.back: The two goods are substitutes; a rise in the price of one increases the demand for the other.

subject: Economics
title: Income Elasticity of Demand
formulaOrRule: $$e_y = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q}{\%\,\Delta Y}$$
derivationOrExplanation: Income elasticity shows the responsiveness of demand to a change in consumer income. Normal goods have positive income elasticity; inferior goods have negative. Among normal goods, necessities have income elasticity between 0 and 1, while luxuries have elasticity greater than 1. This concept helps firms forecast demand during economic growth or recession and assists governments in understanding consumption patterns.

flashcard.front: How does income elasticity distinguish between luxury and necessity goods?
flashcard.back: Luxury goods: e_y > 1; Necessity goods: 0 < e_y < 1.

subject: Economics
title: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED)
formulaOrRule: $$e_d = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q}{\%\,\Delta P} = \frac{\Delta Q / Q}{\Delta P / P}$$

variablesOrTerms.e_d: Price elasticity of demand (negative sign often ignored for magnitude)

derivationOrExplanation: Elasticity measures responsiveness. Percentage change removes units so different goods can be compared. |e_d| > 1 is elastic, = 1 unitary, < 1 inelastic. Point elasticity uses calculus: e_d = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q). Arc elasticity uses mid-point formula for larger changes.

flashcard.back: e_d = (% ΔQ) / (% ΔP). |e_d| > 1 means demand is elastic (quantity responds more than proportionately to price).

subject: Economics
title: Price Elasticity of Supply (PES)

subject: Economics
title: Market Equilibrium – Demand-Supply Interaction
formulaOrRule: Equilibrium price is determined at the intersection of market demand and market supply curves, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Excess demand raises price; excess supply lowers price.

variablesOrTerms.Excess Demand: QD > QS → upward pressure on price
variablesOrTerms.Excess Supply: QS > QD → downward pressure on price

derivationOrExplanation: In a competitive market the interaction of demand and supply forces establishes an equilibrium price and quantity. If price is above equilibrium, surplus (excess supply) appears and sellers compete by lowering price. If price is below equilibrium, shortage (excess demand) appears and buyers bid the price up. The process continues until equilibrium is restored (assuming free market forces).

flashcard.front: What happens in the market when the prevailing price is higher than the equilibrium price?
flashcard.back: Excess supply (surplus) emerges; sellers lower the price until equilibrium is restored.

subject: Economics
title: Producer Equilibrium under Different Market Forms
formulaOrRule: In all market forms the necessary condition is MR = MC. The sufficient condition is that MC should be rising (or the MC curve should cut the MR curve from below).

variablesOrTerms.Sufficient condition: MC is rising at the point of equality

derivationOrExplanation: Whether the firm is a price taker (perfect competition) or a price maker (monopoly, monopolistic competition), profit is maximised at the output where the last unit adds as much to revenue as it does to cost. The second condition ensures that producing more would reduce profit (MC would exceed MR). Under perfect competition this occurs at the minimum point of the AC curve in the long run; under imperfect competition it generally occurs on the falling part of the AC curve (excess capacity).

flashcard.front: State the necessary and sufficient conditions for producer’s equilibrium.
flashcard.back: Necessary: MR = MC. Sufficient: MC is rising (MC cuts MR from below).

subject: Economics
title: Law of Variable Proportions (Returns to a Factor)
formulaOrRule: As more units of a variable factor are combined with fixed factors, Marginal Product first rises, then falls, and may become negative. Three stages: Increasing, Diminishing, Negative returns.

variablesOrTerms.AP: Average Product = TP / units of variable factor
variablesOrTerms.MP: Marginal Product = ΔTP / Δ variable factor

derivationOrExplanation: In the short run at least one factor is fixed. Initially better utilisation of fixed factors raises MP (Stage 1). After the optimum combination, MP declines (Stage 2 – diminishing returns). Further addition causes overcrowding and negative MP (Stage 3). Rational producer operates in Stage 2.

flashcard.front: Name the three stages of the Law of Variable Proportions and state in which stage a rational producer operates.
flashcard.back: Increasing returns, Diminishing returns, Negative returns. Rational producer operates in Stage 2 (diminishing returns).

subject: Economics
title: Returns to a Factor vs Returns to Scale – Quick Comparison
formulaOrRule: Returns to a Factor: short-run concept; only one input varies. Returns to Scale: long-run concept; all inputs vary proportionately.

variablesOrTerms.Returns to a Factor: Law of Variable Proportions (Increasing, Diminishing, Negative)
variablesOrTerms.Returns to Scale: Increasing, Constant, Decreasing returns to scale

derivationOrExplanation: The two concepts operate in different time horizons and under different assumptions about factor variability. Confusion between them is common. Returns to a factor explain the U-shape of short-run marginal and average cost curves. Returns to scale explain the shape of the long-run average cost curve. Both are essential for understanding firm behaviour in the short and long run.

flashcard.front: In which time period does the Law of Variable Proportions operate and why?
flashcard.back: Short run, because at least one factor of production remains fixed while others are varied.

subject: Economics
title: Revenue Curves under Monopoly
formulaOrRule: AR slopes downward (market demand curve). MR also slopes downward and lies below AR; MR is steeper. TR first rises, reaches maximum when MR = 0, then falls.

variablesOrTerms.Price Maker: Monopolist can choose price-output combination on the demand curve
variablesOrTerms.MR < AR: Because price must be lowered on all units to sell an extra unit

derivationOrExplanation: A monopolist faces the entire market demand curve, which is downward-sloping. To sell more, price must be reduced on every unit, so the additional revenue (MR) is less than the price (AR). When MR becomes zero, TR is at its peak. The monopolist never produces in the inelastic portion of demand (where MR is negative).

flashcard.front: Why does the MR curve of a monopolist lie below the AR curve?
flashcard.back: To sell an additional unit the monopolist must reduce the price on all units previously sold; the loss on those units makes MR lower than the new price (AR).

Active Recall: Q: Why does the MR curve of a monopolist lie below the AR curve? | A: To sell an additional unit the monopolist must reduce the price on all units previously sold; the loss on those units makes MR lower than the new price (AR).

Profit maximisation occurs where this horizontal MR equals rising MC.

flashcard.back: AR = MR = Price; all three are represented by the same horizontal straight line.

subject: Economics
title: Determinants of Supply (Shift Factors)
formulaOrRule: Supply curve shifts due to changes in: input prices, technology, taxes & subsidies, prices of related goods, expectations, number of firms, natural factors.

variablesOrTerms.Movement along supply curve: Caused by change in the price of the good itself
variablesOrTerms.Shift of supply curve: Caused by change in any non-price determinant

subject: Business Studies
title: Life Insurance vs General Insurance
formulaOrRule: Life Insurance: contract of assurance; covers human life; principle of indemnity does not apply; long-term; investment element present. General Insurance: contract of indemnity; covers property, liability, health, etc.; usually short-term; pure risk protection.

variablesOrTerms.Indemnity: Compensation limited to actual financial loss (general insurance)

derivationOrExplanation: Life insurance policies (whole life, endowment, term, ULIP) provide financial protection to dependents and often include a savings component. General insurance (fire, marine, motor, health, liability) compensates for actual loss and is subject to the principle of indemnity, contribution and subrogation. Both require insurable interest and utmost good faith.

flashcard.front: Why is the principle of indemnity not applicable to life insurance?
flashcard.back: Because human life cannot be valued in money terms; the sum assured is paid in full on the happening of the event, not limited to ‘actual loss’.

subject: Business Studies
title: Risks and Security Concerns in E-Business
formulaOrRule: Major risks: transaction security (data interception, fraud), data storage & privacy, system reliability, intellectual property issues, and uncertain legal jurisdiction.

variablesOrTerms.Encryption: Conversion of data into coded form to prevent unauthorised access
variablesOrTerms.Digital Signature: Electronic authentication of identity and integrity of a message
variablesOrTerms.SSL / TLS: Protocols that secure data transmission over the internet

derivationOrExplanation: While e-business offers speed and reach, it also exposes firms and customers to cyber risks. Security measures include encryption, firewalls, secure sockets layer (SSL), digital certificates, two-factor authentication and regular security audits. Legal frameworks such as the Information Technology Act in India provide some protection, but cross-border enforcement remains challenging. Trust and perceived security strongly influence customer adoption.

flashcard.front: Name three common security measures used in e-business transactions.
flashcard.back: Encryption, digital signatures / certificates, and SSL/TLS secure connection (or two-factor authentication, firewalls).
flashcard.hint: Protecting data in transit and identity.

subject: Business Studies
title: Fayol’s 14 Principles – Scalar Chain & Unity of Command
formulaOrRule: Scalar Chain: Clear line of authority from top to bottom. Unity of Command: Each employee receives orders from only one superior.

variablesOrTerms.Unity of Command: One boss principle to avoid confusion

flashcard.back: Business ethics provides the moral foundation; social responsibility is the practical application of ethical principles towards various stakeholders and society.

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Marginal Cost and Marginal Revenue via Derivatives
formulaOrRule: If $C(x)$ is the total cost function, Marginal Cost $= C'(x)$. If $R(x)$ is the total revenue function, Marginal Revenue $= R'(x)$. Profit $\pi(x) = R(x) - C(x)$; maximum when $\pi'(x) = 0$ and $\pi''(x) < 0$.

variablesOrTerms.C'(x): Derivative of total cost = instantaneous rate of change of cost
variablesOrTerms.R'(x): Derivative of total revenue = instantaneous rate of change of revenue

derivationOrExplanation: In economics, marginal cost and marginal revenue are the derivatives of the respective total functions. Setting MR = MC (i.e., R'(x) = C'(x)) gives the critical point for profit maximisation. The second-derivative test confirms whether it is a maximum. These applications link calculus directly to managerial decision-making.

flashcard.front: How is marginal cost obtained from the total cost function using calculus?
flashcard.back: Marginal cost is the first derivative of the total cost function: MC = C'(x).

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Spearman’s Rank Correlation Coefficient
formulaOrRule: $$r_s = 1 - \frac{6\sum d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)}$$ where $d_i$ = difference in ranks of the i-th pair.

variablesOrTerms.d_i: Difference between the ranks of the two variables for each observation

derivationOrExplanation: When data are qualitative or when the relationship is monotonic but not necessarily linear, Spearman’s rank correlation is preferred. Observations are ranked and the differences in ranks are squared and summed. The formula yields a value between −1 and +1. It is less sensitive to outliers than Pearson’s coefficient and can be used with ordinal data.

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Ordinary Annuity vs Annuity Due
formulaOrRule: Ordinary Annuity: payments at end of each period. Annuity Due: payments at beginning of each period. PV and FV of annuity due = corresponding value of ordinary annuity × (1 + i).

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Simple Interest vs Compound Interest – Comparison
formulaOrRule: Simple Interest: $$SI = \frac{P \times R \times T}{100}$$ (interest only on original principal). Compound Interest: interest is calculated on principal plus previously accumulated interest.

variablesOrTerms.Conversion period: Frequency with which interest is compounded

derivationOrExplanation: Under simple interest the interest amount remains constant each year. Under compound interest the effective principal grows, so interest grows over time. Effective rate can be calculated to compare different compounding frequencies.

flashcard.front: Why is compound interest greater than simple interest for the same principal, rate and time (when time > 1 period)?
flashcard.back: Because under compound interest, interest of previous periods is added to the principal and itself earns interest in subsequent periods.

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Chain Rule of Differentiation
formulaOrRule: If $y = f(u)$ and $u = g(x)$, then $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}$$
derivationOrExplanation: Many functions in commerce and economics are composite (e.g., cost as a function of output which itself depends on time). The chain rule allows differentiation without expanding the expression. It is the foundation for implicit differentiation and related-rates problems. In marginal analysis it helps find the rate of change of one economic variable with respect to another through intermediate variables.

flashcard.front: State the chain rule for differentiation.
flashcard.back: If y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du) × (du/dx).

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Combination Formula
formulaOrRule: $$C(n,r) = \binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} = \frac{P(n,r)}{r!}$$

variablesOrTerms.C(n,r): Number of ways to choose r objects out of n without regard to order

derivationOrExplanation: Combination counts selections where order is irrelevant. Since each selection of r objects can be arranged in r! ways, we divide P(n,r) by r!. Useful identity: $C(n,r) = C(n,n-r)$. Pascal’s identity: $C(n,r) = C(n-1,r-1) + C(n-1,r)$.

flashcard.front: Write the relation between P(n,r) and C(n,r).
flashcard.back: $C(n,r) = P(n,r) / r!$ or $P(n,r) = C(n,r) \times r!$.

title: Permutation Formula

variablesOrTerms.r: Number of objects taken at a time

derivationOrExplanation: Permutation counts arrangements where order matters. First place can be filled in n ways, second in (n−1) ways, and so on down to (n−r+1). Factorial form is compact. title: Binomial Probability Distribution (Introductory)

variablesOrTerms.Binomial experiment: Fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with constant probability of success

derivationOrExplanation: The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each having the same probability of success. The mean and variance are simply np and npq respectively.

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Independent Events – Multiplication Rule
formulaOrRule: Events A and B are independent if $$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$$. Consequently $$P(A|B) = P(A)$$ and $$P(B|A) = P(B)$$.

variablesOrTerms.Independent Events: Occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other
variablesOrTerms.Dependent Events: Occurrence of one changes the probability of the other

derivationOrExplanation: Independence is a stronger condition than mutual exclusiveness. Mutually exclusive events with positive probability cannot be independent. The multiplication rule for independent events simplifies many calculations in successive draws with replacement, coin tosses, and quality-control sampling. In real life, true independence must be carefully justified.

flashcard.front: Write the multiplication rule for two independent events A and B.
flashcard.back: $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)$

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Types of Functions – One-one, Onto, Bijective
formulaOrRule: One-one (injective): $f(x_1)=f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1=x_2$. Onto (surjective): Range = Codomain. Bijective: both one-one and onto.

variablesOrTerms.Domain: Set of all possible input values
variablesOrTerms.Codomain: Set of all possible output values declared
variablesOrTerms.Range: Actual set of output values obtained

derivationOrExplanation: A function assigns to each element of domain exactly one element of codomain. One-one means different inputs give different outputs. Onto means every element of codomain is hit. Only bijective functions have inverse functions. Horizontal line test checks one-one; range check checks onto.

flashcard.front: When is a function bijective? Why is bijectivity important?
flashcard.back: When it is both one-one and onto. Only bijective functions possess an inverse function.

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Applications of Geometric Progression in Finance
formulaOrRule: Compound interest, present value of growing annuities, and depreciation under WDV method all follow geometric sequences.

variablesOrTerms.Growth factor: 1 + r (where r is the periodic rate)
variablesOrTerms.WDV depreciation: Book value forms a GP with common ratio (1 − rate)

flashcard.back: Successive book values form a GP with first term = original cost and common ratio = (1 − depreciation rate).

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Geometric Progression – nth Term and Sum
formulaOrRule: $$a_n = ar^{n-1}$$\quad $$S_n = a\frac{r^n-1}{r-1}\ (r\neq 1)$$\quad $$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}\ (|r|<1)$$
derivationOrExplanation: Each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by constant r. Sum formula is derived by multiplying S_n by r and subtracting: $S_n - rS_n = a - ar^n$. flashcard.back: $S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}$ provided $|r| < 1$.

title: Sum of n terms of an Arithmetic Progression
formulaOrRule: $$S_n = \frac{n}{2}\bigl[2a + (n-1)d\bigr] = \frac{n}{2}(a + l)$$

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Set Operations – Union, Intersection, Complement
formulaOrRule: $$A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$$\quad $$A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$$\quad $$A' = \{x : x \notin A\}$$

variablesOrTerms.A': Complement of A (with respect to universal set U)

derivationOrExplanation: Union contains all elements that belong to at least one of the sets. Intersection contains only common elements. Complement contains elements of the universal set that are not in A. De Morgan’s laws: $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$. Venn diagrams are used for visualisation.

flashcard.front: State De Morgan’s laws for two sets A and B.
flashcard.back: $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$.

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Absolute vs Relative Measures of Dispersion
formulaOrRule: Absolute measures (Range, Quartile Deviation, Mean Deviation, Standard Deviation) are expressed in the same unit as the variable. Relative measures (Coefficient of Range, QD, MD, Variation) are pure numbers and used for comparison across different units or magnitudes.
derivationOrExplanation: When two data sets have different units or widely different means, absolute measures cannot be compared directly. Relative measures standardise the dispersion by dividing by a central value (usually the mean). title: Inventory Turnover and Trade Receivables Turnover
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Inventory Turnover Ratio} = \frac{\text{Cost of Revenue from Operations}}{\text{Average Inventory}}$$\quad $$\text{Trade Receivables Turnover} = \frac{\text{Net Credit Revenue from Operations}}{\text{Average Trade Receivables}}$$
derivationOrExplanation: Activity ratios measure how efficiently the enterprise is using its assets. Inventory Turnover indicates how many times inventory is converted into sales during the year; a higher ratio generally means efficient inventory management. Trade Receivables Turnover shows how quickly credit sales are converted into cash; a higher ratio (or lower collection period) indicates efficient credit and collection policy. These ratios help in assessing operational efficiency.

flashcard.front: What does a high Inventory Turnover Ratio generally indicate?
flashcard.back: Efficient inventory management – inventory is being sold and replenished quickly.

subject: Accountancy
title: Current Ratio and Quick Ratio
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Current Ratio} = \frac{\text{Current Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$$\quad $$\text{Quick Ratio} = \frac{\text{Quick Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$$\quad $$\text{Quick Assets} = \text{Current Assets} - \text{Inventory} - \text{Prepaid Expenses}$$
derivationOrExplanation: Current ratio measures the ability to meet short-term obligations from all current assets. Quick ratio is a stricter test because it excludes inventory and prepaid expenses, which are less readily convertible into cash. A high current ratio with a low quick ratio may indicate overstocking. Both ratios are key indicators of short-term solvency and liquidity risk.

flashcard.front: Write the formulas for Current Ratio and Quick Ratio and state their ideal values.
flashcard.back: Current Ratio = CA / CL (ideal 2:1); Quick Ratio = (CA − Inventory − Prepaid) / CL (ideal 1:1).

subject: Accountancy
title: Gross Profit Ratio, Net Profit Ratio and ROCE
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Gross Profit Ratio} = \frac{\text{Gross Profit}}{\text{Revenue from Operations}} \times 100$$\quad $$\text{Net Profit Ratio} = \frac{\text{Net Profit}}{\text{Revenue from Operations}} \times 100$$\quad $$\text{ROCE} = \frac{\text{EBIT}}{\text{Capital Employed}} \times 100$$

flashcard.back: ROCE = (EBIT / Capital Employed) × 100.

subject: Accountancy
title: Debt-Equity Ratio and Proprietary Ratio
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Debt-Equity Ratio} = \frac{\text{Long-term Debt}}{\text{Shareholders' Funds}}$$\quad $$\text{Proprietary Ratio} = \frac{\text{Shareholders' Funds}}{\text{Total Assets}}$$

subject: Accountancy
title: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
formulaOrRule: Net Profit (from P&L) is appropriated in the order: Interest on Capital, Partner’s Salary/Commission, Interest on Partner’s Loan (if any), then divisible profit shared in profit-sharing ratio. Interest on Drawings is credited to the Appropriation A/c.

variablesOrTerms.Profit & Loss Appropriation A/c: Extension of P&L Account used only by partnership firms to distribute profit among partners

derivationOrExplanation: Unlike a sole proprietorship, a partnership must show how net profit is distributed among partners according to the partnership deed. Appropriations such as interest on capital and salary are charges against profit only if the deed permits; otherwise they are appropriations. The final balance (divisible profit or loss) is transferred to the partners’ capital or current accounts in the agreed ratio.

flashcard.front: What is the purpose of the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?
flashcard.back: To show the distribution of net profit among partners after allowing interest on capital, salary, commission and charging interest on drawings.

subject: Accountancy
title: Features of Partnership and Partnership Deed
formulaOrRule: Partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932). Partnership Deed is the written agreement containing terms of partnership.

variablesOrTerms.Mutual Agency: Every partner is both an agent and a principal of the firm
variablesOrTerms.Unlimited Liability: Partners are jointly and severally liable for firm’s debts (except in LLP)
variablesOrTerms.Partnership Deed: Document specifying name, nature of business, capital, PSR, interest on capital/drawings, salary, etc.

derivationOrExplanation: In the absence of a Partnership Deed, the following rules of the Indian Partnership Act apply: profits and losses shared equally, no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, no salary to partners, 6% p.a. interest on partner’s loan. A written deed avoids disputes and provides clarity on rights and duties. Registration of the firm is optional but advisable for legal benefits.

flashcard.front: In the absence of a Partnership Deed, how are profits shared and is interest on capital allowed?
flashcard.back: Profits and losses are shared equally; no interest on capital is allowed.
flashcard.hint: Default rules of the Partnership Act.

subject: Accountancy
title: Forfeiture and Reissue of Shares
formulaOrRule: On Forfeiture: Debit Share Capital A/c (with called-up amount), Credit Share Forfeiture A/c (with amount received), Credit Calls-in-Arrears / respective Call A/c (with unpaid amount). On Reissue: Debit Bank, Debit Share Forfeiture (if reissued at discount), Credit Share Capital. Balance of Share Forfeiture after reissue is transferred to Capital Reserve.

variablesOrTerms.Forfeiture: Cancellation of shares for non-payment of calls
variablesOrTerms.Capital Reserve: Capital profit arising from forfeiture of shares that is not available for dividend

derivationOrExplanation: When a shareholder fails to pay calls, the company may forfeit the shares after giving due notice. The amount already received is transferred to Share Forfeiture Account. Forfeited shares can be reissued at par, premium or discount (discount not exceeding the amount forfeited). Any surplus remaining in Share Forfeiture Account after reissue is a capital profit and is transferred to Capital Reserve. Loss on reissue cannot exceed the forfeited amount.

flashcard.front: What happens to the balance left in Share Forfeiture Account after reissue of forfeited shares?
flashcard.back: It is transferred to Capital Reserve Account as it represents a capital profit.

subject: Accountancy
title: Issue of Shares at Par and at Premium
formulaOrRule: At Par: Debit Bank, Credit Share Application/Allotment/Call A/c; then transfer to Share Capital A/c. At Premium: Additional amount credited to Securities Premium A/c (under Section 52 of Companies Act, 2013).

variablesOrTerms.Securities Premium: Amount received in excess of face value; can be used only for specific purposes (bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, premium on redemption, buy-back, etc.)

derivationOrExplanation: Shares may be issued at par (equal to face value), at premium (above face value) or at discount (below face value – now generally prohibited for fresh issue). Premium is a capital profit and is credited to Securities Premium Account. The Companies Act restricts the utilisation of securities premium. Accounting involves separate stages: application, allotment and calls. Over-subscription and under-subscription require pro-rata allotment or refund adjustments.

flashcard.front: Where is the amount of securities premium credited and what are its permitted uses?
flashcard.back: Credited to Securities Premium Account. Permitted uses include issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back of shares.

subject: Accountancy
title: Pro-rata Allotment in Case of Over-Subscription
formulaOrRule: When shares are over-subscribed, allotment is made proportionately. Excess application money is adjusted towards allotment and further calls; any remaining excess is refunded.

variablesOrTerms.Over-subscription: Number of shares applied for > Number of shares offered
variablesOrTerms.Pro-rata Allotment: Allotment in proportion to shares applied for

derivationOrExplanation: In case of over-subscription the company may reject some applications, accept some in full, and accept the rest on a pro-rata basis. Excess money received on pro-rata applications is first adjusted towards the amount due on allotment and subsequent calls. Only the surplus after full adjustment is refunded. Accurate calculation of the proportion and the excess amount per share is essential for correct journal entries.

flashcard.front: What is pro-rata allotment and how is excess application money treated?
flashcard.back: Allotment of shares in proportion to the number applied for. Excess application money is adjusted towards allotment (and calls) and any balance is refunded.

subject: Accountancy
title: Revaluation Account and Treatment of Reserves on Admission
formulaOrRule: Revaluation A/c is prepared to record increase/decrease in asset values and recording of unrecorded assets/liabilities. Profit or loss on revaluation is transferred to old partners in old ratio. Accumulated reserves and profits are also distributed to old partners in old ratio.

variablesOrTerms.Revaluation Account: Nominal account that ascertains profit or loss due to revaluation of assets and liabilities

derivationOrExplanation: At the time of admission, assets and liabilities are revalued so that the new partner does not benefit from or suffer due to unrecorded changes. Any profit on revaluation belongs to the old partners. Similarly, general reserve, accumulated profits and losses appearing in the balance sheet are distributed among old partners in the old ratio before the new partner is admitted. The new partner’s capital is credited with the amount brought in.

flashcard.front: In which ratio is the profit or loss on revaluation transferred at the time of admission of a partner?
flashcard.back: In the old profit-sharing ratio among the old partners.
flashcard.hint: New partner should not share past revaluation gains/losses.

subject: Accountancy
title: Treatment of Goodwill on Admission
formulaOrRule: New partner brings his share of goodwill in cash (premium) → credited to sacrificing partners in sacrificing ratio. If goodwill is not brought in cash, it is adjusted through capital accounts (gaining partners debited, sacrificing partners credited).

variablesOrTerms.Premium for Goodwill: Amount brought by new partner for his share of goodwill

derivationOrExplanation: The new partner acquires a share in the future profits and therefore compensates the old partners for the sacrifice of their share. When goodwill is brought in cash, it is shared by the sacrificing partners. When it is not brought in cash, the adjustment is made through the capital accounts so that the sacrificing partners’ capitals increase and the new partner’s capital (or the gaining partners’) decreases accordingly. Hidden goodwill is inferred when the total capital of the firm is implied by the new partner’s capital contribution.

flashcard.front: When a new partner brings his share of goodwill in cash, how is it distributed?
flashcard.back: It is credited to the sacrificing partners in their sacrificing ratio.
flashcard.hint: Compensation for sacrifice of profit share.

subject: Accountancy
title: Cash Flow from Operating Activities – Indirect Method
formulaOrRule: Net Profit before Tax + Non-cash expenses (Depreciation, Amortisation) − Non-operating incomes +/− Changes in Working Capital (Current Assets & Current Liabilities) − Tax Paid = Net Cash from Operating Activities.

variablesOrTerms.Non-cash expenses: Expenses that do not involve cash outflow (depreciation, preliminary expenses written off)
variablesOrTerms.Working Capital adjustments: Increase in CA → outflow; Increase in CL → inflow

derivationOrExplanation: The indirect method starts with accrual-based net profit and converts it to a cash basis. Non-cash charges are added back; non-operating items are adjusted; and changes in current assets and liabilities are reflected to arrive at actual cash generated by core operations. This figure is crucial for assessing the firm’s ability to generate cash from its primary activities and to meet obligations without external financing.

flashcard.front: Why is depreciation added back while calculating cash flow from operating activities under the indirect method?
flashcard.back: Because depreciation is a non-cash expense that reduced net profit but did not involve any cash outflow.

subject: Accountancy
title: Classification of Business Activities in Cash Flow Statement
formulaOrRule: Operating Activities: principal revenue-producing activities. Investing Activities: acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments. Financing Activities: changes in size and composition of owners’ capital and borrowings.

variablesOrTerms.Operating Activities: Cash from customers, payment to suppliers, employees, taxes, etc.
variablesOrTerms.Investing Activities: Purchase/sale of fixed assets, investments, interest/dividend received (in some treatments)
variablesOrTerms.Financing Activities: Issue of shares/debentures, repayment of loans, payment of dividend and interest on loans

derivationOrExplanation: AS-3 (or Ind AS-7) requires classification of cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities. This classification helps users assess the ability of the enterprise to generate cash from operations, its investment and financing strategy, and its overall liquidity. Non-cash transactions (e.g., conversion of debentures into shares) are disclosed separately in a note.

Formula / Rule: Operating Activities: principal revenue-producing activities. Investing Activities: acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments. Financing Activities: changes in size and composition of owners’ capital and borrowings.

Explanation: AS-3 (or Ind AS-7) requires classification of cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities. subject: Accountancy
title: Steps in Preparing Cash Flow from Operating Activities (Indirect Method)
formulaOrRule: Start with Net Profit before Tax → Add non-cash and non-operating expenses → Deduct non-operating incomes → Adjust for changes in working capital (Current Assets & Current Liabilities) → Deduct Tax Paid = Net Cash from Operating Activities.

variablesOrTerms.Non-cash expenses: Depreciation, amortisation, preliminary expenses written off, provision for doubtful debts (if created)
variablesOrTerms.Working capital changes: Increase in current assets = outflow; Increase in current liabilities = inflow

derivationOrExplanation: The indirect method reconciles accrual-based net profit with cash generated from operations. Non-cash charges that reduced profit are added back. Non-operating items (interest, dividend, profit/loss on sale of assets) are adjusted to isolate operating cash flows. Changes in working capital reflect the cash impact of day-to-day operations. Tax paid is deducted to arrive at the final operating cash flow figure.

flashcard.front: List the main adjustments made to Net Profit while calculating cash from operating activities under the indirect method.
flashcard.back: Add non-cash expenses, deduct non-operating incomes, adjust for changes in current assets and current liabilities, and deduct tax paid.

subject: Accountancy
title: Calculation of Amount Due to Deceased Partner
formulaOrRule: Amount due = Capital + Share of Goodwill + Share of Reserves + Share of Revaluation Profit + Share of Profit up to date of death + Interest on Capital − Drawings − Interest on Drawings − Share of Revaluation Loss.

variablesOrTerms.Executor’s Account: Account to which the final amount due is transferred
variablesOrTerms.Profit up to date of death: Estimated on the basis of previous year’s profit or average profit or turnover basis

derivationOrExplanation: The legal representative (executor) of the deceased partner is entitled to the partner’s share of capital, reserves, goodwill, revaluation and profit earned till the date of death. Profit till the date of death is calculated either on time basis (previous year’s profit × months/12) or on turnover basis. The final amount is transferred to the Executor’s Account and settled according to the partnership deed or legal provisions.

flashcard.front: How is the deceased partner’s share of profit till the date of death usually calculated?
flashcard.back: On the basis of previous year’s profit (time basis) or on the basis of turnover (sales basis), as agreed.

subject: Accountancy
title: Realisation Account and Settlement of Accounts
formulaOrRule: Realisation A/c is opened to close asset and liability accounts (except cash/bank and partners’ capitals). Assets are realised, liabilities are paid, and the resulting profit or loss is transferred to partners’ capital accounts in the profit-sharing ratio. Partners’ capitals are then settled.

variablesOrTerms.Realisation Account: Nominal account that ascertains profit or loss on realisation of assets and payment of liabilities
variablesOrTerms.Memorandum Balance Sheet: Sometimes prepared to find missing figures

derivationOrExplanation: On dissolution the firm’s assets are sold and liabilities are paid off. Realisation Account helps determine the profit or loss on this process. Unrecorded assets and liabilities are also accounted for. After transferring realisation profit/loss and settling partner’s loans, the final balances of capital accounts are paid off or recovered. The Garner vs Murray rule (applicable in some cases of insolvency) requires solvent partners to bear the deficiency of an insolvent partner in the ratio of their capitals.

flashcard.front: What is the purpose of preparing a Realisation Account on dissolution of a firm?
flashcard.back: To ascertain the profit or loss on realisation of assets and payment of liabilities, which is then transferred to partners’ capital accounts.
flashcard.hint: Closing the books of the firm.

subject: Accountancy
title: Issue of Debentures at Par, Premium and Discount
formulaOrRule: Debentures can be issued at par, at premium or at discount. Discount on issue is a capital loss and is written off over the life of debentures (or from Securities Premium). Interest on debentures is a charge against profit and is paid at a fixed rate on face value.

variablesOrTerms.Debenture: Instrument acknowledging debt; may be secured or unsecured, redeemable or irredeemable, convertible or non-convertible

derivationOrExplanation: Unlike shares, debentures represent borrowed funds. They carry fixed interest obligation regardless of profit. Issue at discount creates a capital loss that is amortised over the period till redemption. Interest is credited to Debenture-holders periodically and is tax-deductible. Debentures may be redeemable at par or at premium; the premium on redemption is also provided for over the life of the debentures.

flashcard.front: Is interest on debentures a charge against profit or an appropriation of profit?
flashcard.back: It is a charge against profit (paid even if there is a loss).

subject: Accountancy
title: Sacrificing Ratio on Admission of a Partner
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Sacrificing Ratio} = \text{Old Ratio} - \text{New Ratio}$$

variablesOrTerms.Sacrificing Ratio: Ratio in which old partners surrender their share of profit in favour of the new partner
variablesOrTerms.Gaining Ratio: Used at retirement/death; opposite of sacrificing ratio

derivationOrExplanation: When a new partner is admitted, the old partners sacrifice a portion of their profit share. The sacrificing ratio is used to distribute the goodwill brought in by the new partner (or the goodwill adjusted through capital accounts). It is calculated by deducting the new profit-sharing ratio from the old ratio for each old partner. Only the sacrificing partners are credited for goodwill.

flashcard.front: How is the sacrificing ratio calculated on admission of a new partner?
flashcard.back: Sacrificing Ratio = Old Ratio − New Ratio (for each old partner).
flashcard.hint: Difference between old and new shares.

subject: Accountancy
topic: Reconstitution – Change in Profit Sharing Ratio
title: Adjustment for Change in Profit Sharing Ratio
formulaOrRule: Sacrificing Ratio = Old Ratio − New Ratio. Gaining Ratio = New Ratio − Old Ratio. Goodwill is adjusted through Partners’ Capital Accounts in sacrificing/gaining ratio (without opening Goodwill A/c in many cases).
derivationOrExplanation: When partners decide to change their profit-sharing ratio, the gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner for the sacrifice of share in profits (and inherent goodwill). The adjustment is usually made by debiting the gaining partners’ capital accounts and crediting the sacrificing partners’ capital accounts with the proportionate amount of goodwill. Reserves, accumulated profits/losses and revaluation of assets/liabilities are also adjusted in the old ratio before the change.

flashcard.front: How is goodwill adjusted when there is a change in profit-sharing ratio among existing partners?
flashcard.back: Gaining partners’ capital accounts are debited and sacrificing partners’ capital accounts are credited in the gaining/sacrificing ratio with the share of goodwill.

subject: Accountancy
title: Common-Size Financial Statements
formulaOrRule: Each item is expressed as a percentage of a common base. In the Income Statement the base is Revenue from Operations (Net Sales). In the Balance Sheet the base is Total Assets (or Total Liabilities & Equity).

variablesOrTerms.Common Base: 100 % figure against which all other items are expressed

derivationOrExplanation: Common-size statements eliminate the effect of size and facilitate comparison between firms of different sizes or between different periods of the same firm. They reveal the internal structure and relative importance of various items. For example, a rising percentage of cost of goods sold to sales indicates declining gross margin. Common-size analysis is particularly useful for inter-firm comparison.

flashcard.front: What is the common base used in a Common-Size Income Statement and a Common-Size Balance Sheet?
flashcard.back: Income Statement: Revenue from Operations (Net Sales). Balance Sheet: Total Assets (or Total of Equity and Liabilities).

title: Comparative Financial Statements
formulaOrRule: Comparative statements show figures of two or more periods side by side together with absolute change and percentage change. Percentage change = (Absolute change / Figure of previous period) × 100.

variablesOrTerms.Horizontal Analysis: Another name for comparative analysis across periods

subject: Accountancy
title: Main Methods of Valuing Goodwill
formulaOrRule: 1. Average Profit Method: Goodwill = Average Profit × Years’ Purchase. 2. Super Profit Method: Goodwill = Super Profit × Years’ Purchase. 3. Capitalisation Method: (a) Capitalisation of Average Profit, (b) Capitalisation of Super Profit.

variablesOrTerms.Average Profit: Simple or weighted average of past adjusted profits
variablesOrTerms.Normal Profit: Capital Employed × Normal Rate of Return / 100

derivationOrExplanation: Goodwill is the value of the firm’s reputation and ability to earn super profits. Average Profit Method assumes future maintainable profits equal past average. Super Profit Method recognises only excess over normal return. Capitalisation of Average Profit gives total firm value; goodwill is total value minus capital employed. Capitalisation of Super Profit directly capitalises the excess earnings. Choice of method depends on the nature of business and agreement among partners.

flashcard.front: Name the three main methods of valuing goodwill.
flashcard.back: Average Profit Method, Super Profit Method, and Capitalisation Method (of Average Profit or Super Profit).
flashcard.hint: Based on past profits and normal return.

title: Super Profit Method of Goodwill Valuation
formulaOrRule: $$\text{Goodwill} = \text{Super Profit} \times \text{Number of Years' Purchase}$$\quad $$\text{Super Profit} = \text{Average Profit} - \text{Normal Profit}$$\quad $$\text{Normal Profit} = \text{Capital Employed} \times \frac{\text{Normal Rate of Return}}{100}$$

subject: Economics
title: Investment Multiplier – Derivation and Working
formulaOrRule: $$k = \frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta I} = \frac{1}{1 - \text{MPC}} = \frac{1}{\text{MPS}}$$
derivationOrExplanation: An initial increase in investment generates an equal increase in income. Recipients of this income spend a fraction (MPC) and save the rest (MPS). The spent portion becomes income for the next round of recipients, and the process continues. The total change in income is the sum of an infinite geometric series: ΔI + ΔI·MPC + ΔI·MPC² + … = ΔI / (1 − MPC). Higher MPC (lower MPS) produces a larger multiplier. Leakages (saving, taxes, imports) reduce the value of the multiplier.

flashcard.front: Derive the relationship between the multiplier and MPC.
flashcard.back: k = 1 / (1 − MPC). The higher the MPC, the larger the multiplier.

subject: Economics
title: Measures of Money Supply in India (RBI)
formulaOrRule: M1 = Currency with public + Demand deposits + Other deposits with RBI. M2 = M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office. M3 = M1 + Time deposits with banks (Broad Money). M4 = M3 + Total deposits with Post Office.

variablesOrTerms.M3: Broad Money – most commonly used aggregate

derivationOrExplanation: RBI publishes four alternative measures of money supply with decreasing liquidity. M1 is the most liquid and is closely related to transactions demand. M3 is the widely used broad money measure for policy analysis. Changes in money supply influence interest rates, inflation and economic activity. RBI uses instruments such as repo rate, CRR, SLR and open-market operations to regulate money supply.

flashcard.front: What is the difference between M1 and M3?
flashcard.back: M1 is narrow money (currency + demand deposits). M3 is broad money (M1 + time deposits of the public with banks).

subject: Economics
title: Three Methods of Measuring National Income
formulaOrRule: Value Added Method (Product): Sum of net value added by all producing units. Income Method: Sum of factor incomes (Compensation of employees + Rent + Interest + Profit + Mixed income). Expenditure Method: C + I + G + (X − M).
derivationOrExplanation: All three methods should theoretically give the same result (National Income). In practice, statistical discrepancies arise. Value-added method avoids double counting by excluding intermediate consumption. Income method sums incomes earned by factors of production. Expenditure method sums spending on final goods and services. Net Indirect Taxes and Net Factor Income from Abroad are adjusted according to the aggregate required (GDP, NDP, GNP, NNP, etc.).

flashcard.back: Value Added (Product) Method, Income Method, and Expenditure Method.

subject: Business Studies
title: Capital Structure – Factors and Trading on Equity
formulaOrRule: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity. Trading on Equity (Financial Leverage) is favourable when ROI > Interest rate on debt, increasing return on equity.

variablesOrTerms.Financial Leverage: Use of debt to magnify return on equity
variablesOrTerms.ROI: Return on Investment / Return on Capital Employed

derivationOrExplanation: Debt is cheaper than equity because interest is tax-deductible and debt-holders take lower risk. However, fixed interest obligation increases financial risk. Optimal capital structure minimises the overall cost of capital while keeping risk at an acceptable level. Factors affecting the choice include cash-flow position, interest coverage, cost of debt and equity, control considerations, flexibility and market conditions.

flashcard.front: When is trading on equity advantageous to equity shareholders?
flashcard.back: When the return on total capital employed is higher than the rate of interest payable on debt.

Subject: Business Studies (Commerce - class_12)
Topic: Financial Management
Formula / Rule: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity. Trading on Equity (Financial Leverage) is favourable when ROI > Interest rate on debt, increasing return on equity.
Variables: Debt-Equity Ratio = Long-term Debt / Shareholders’ Funds; Financial Leverage = Use of debt to magnify return on equity; ROI = Return on Investment / Return on Capital Employed
Explanation: Debt is cheaper than equity because interest is tax-deductible and debt-holders take lower risk. However, fixed interest obligation increases financial risk. Optimal capital structure minimises the overall cost of capital while keeping risk at an acceptable level. Factors affecting the choice include cash-flow position, interest coverage, cost of debt and equity, control considerations, flexibility and market conditions.
Active Recall: Q: When is trading on equity advantageous to equity shareholders? | A: When the return on total capital employed is higher than the rate of interest payable on debt.

subject: Business Studies
title: Working Capital Management – Concept and Factors
formulaOrRule: Gross Working Capital = Total Current Assets; Net Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. Factors: nature of business, production cycle, operating efficiency, credit policy, growth, seasonal factors, availability of raw material.

variablesOrTerms.Permanent Working Capital: Minimum level required throughout the year
variablesOrTerms.Fluctuating Working Capital: Extra capital needed for seasonal or cyclical peaks

derivationOrExplanation: Adequate working capital ensures smooth day-to-day operations and the ability to meet short-term obligations. Excess working capital means idle funds and lower profitability; inadequate working capital leads to liquidity crises and lost opportunities. Efficient management involves controlling inventory, receivables and payables (operating cycle) while arranging appropriate short-term finance.

flashcard.front: Distinguish between Gross and Net Working Capital.
flashcard.back: Gross Working Capital = Total Current Assets; Net Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities.

subject: Applied Mathematics
title: Formulation of a Linear Programming Problem
formulaOrRule: Identify decision variables → Write objective function (Max/Min) → Write constraints as linear inequalities → Add non-negativity restrictions.

variablesOrTerms.Decision Variables: Quantities to be determined (e.g., units of products)
variablesOrTerms.Objective Function: Linear function to be maximised or minimised
variablesOrTerms.Constraints: Limitations on resources expressed as inequalities

derivationOrExplanation: Every LPP begins with careful formulation. Decision variables represent the choices available. The objective function expresses the goal (profit, cost, etc.). Constraints reflect limited resources (labour, material, machine hours, demand). Non-negativity ensures variables cannot be negative. Once formulated, the problem can be solved graphically (two variables) or by simplex method (more variables).

flashcard.front: List the four essential steps in formulating a linear programming problem.
flashcard.back: Identify decision variables, write the objective function, write the constraints, add non-negativity restrictions.
flashcard.hint: From real problem to mathematical model.

subject: Political Science
title: Classification of Directive Principles
formulaOrRule: Socialistic Principles (welfare state goals), Gandhian Principles (village panchayats, cottage industries, prohibition), Liberal-Intellectual Principles (uniform civil code, free legal aid, separation of judiciary from executive).

variablesOrTerms.Article 37: Directive Principles are fundamental in the governance of the country

derivationOrExplanation: DPSPs aim to establish a welfare state and social and economic democracy. Although not enforceable in courts, they guide legislation and policy. Many have been implemented through laws and constitutional amendments (e.g., Panchayati Raj, free education, equal pay). The Supreme Court has held that Fundamental Rights and DPSPs should be interpreted harmoniously.

flashcard.front: Are Directive Principles enforceable in a court of law? What is their constitutional status?
flashcard.back: No, they are non-justiciable. However, Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country.
flashcard.hint: Moral and political obligations on the State.

subject: Political Science
title: Features of Free and Fair Elections in India
formulaOrRule: Universal adult franchise, independent Election Commission, regular elections, secret ballot, level playing field (Model Code of Conduct), judicial oversight, and multi-party competition.

variablesOrTerms.Election Commission of India: Autonomous constitutional body (Art 324) that conducts elections
variablesOrTerms.Model Code of Conduct: Set of guidelines for political parties and candidates during elections

derivationOrExplanation: India’s electoral system is based on universal adult suffrage and the first-past-the-post system for most elections. The Election Commission is independent and has extensive powers to ensure free and fair elections. Challenges include money and muscle power, criminalisation of politics, and misuse of state resources. Reforms such as the introduction of EVMs, VVPAT, and expenditure limits aim to strengthen the integrity of the process.

flashcard.front: Which constitutional body is responsible for conducting free and fair elections in India?
flashcard.back: The Election Commission of India (Article 324).

flashcard.back: No, they are non-justiciable. They provide guidelines for the State to achieve social and economic justice and establish a welfare state.

subject: Political Science
title: Fundamental Rights – Categories and Features
formulaOrRule: Six categories (originally seven): Right to Equality (Arts 14–18), Right to Freedom (19–22), Right against Exploitation (23–24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25–28), Cultural & Educational Rights (29–30), Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). Right to Property was removed (now legal right under Art 300A).

variablesOrTerms.Justiciable: Enforceable in a court of law
variablesOrTerms.Article 32: Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights (Heart and Soul of the Constitution – Ambedkar)

derivationOrExplanation: Fundamental Rights are guaranteed against the state and, in some cases, against private individuals. They are not absolute; reasonable restrictions can be imposed. The Right to Constitutional Remedies makes the other rights meaningful by allowing citizens to approach the Supreme Court or High Courts directly. During Emergency (Art 352) certain rights can be suspended, but Arts 20 and 21 cannot.

flashcard.front: Which Fundamental Right is called the ‘Heart and Soul’ of the Constitution and why?
flashcard.back: Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32), because it makes all other Fundamental Rights enforceable.

subject: Political Science
title: Preamble – Key Words and Significance
formulaOrRule: We, the people of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic and to secure to all its citizens: Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity…

variablesOrTerms.Sovereign: Independent authority, not subject to external control
variablesOrTerms.Socialist: Commitment to social and economic equality (added 1976)
variablesOrTerms.Secular: Equal respect for all religions; no state religion (added 1976)
variablesOrTerms.Democratic: Government based on the will of the people
variablesOrTerms.Republic: Head of State is elected, not hereditary

derivationOrExplanation: The Preamble embodies the basic philosophy and fundamental values of the Constitution. It is not enforceable in a court of law but is used by the judiciary as a guide to interpretation. The words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Preamble declares the source of the Constitution (‘We, the people’) and the objectives the Constitution seeks to achieve.

flashcard.front: What do the terms Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic and Republic in the Preamble signify?
flashcard.back: Sovereign – independent; Socialist – social & economic equality; Secular – equal respect for all religions; Democratic – people’s rule; Republic – elected head of state.

subject: History
title: Causes of the French Revolution (1789)
formulaOrRule: Long-term: Social inequality (Three Estates), absolute monarchy, Enlightenment ideas. Medium-term: Financial crisis, unfair taxation. Immediate: Calling of Estates-General, Tennis Court Oath, Storming of the Bastille.

variablesOrTerms.Third Estate: Commoners (bourgeoisie, peasants, urban workers) – bore the tax burden

derivationOrExplanation: The French Revolution resulted from the interaction of structural inequalities of the Ancien Régime, a severe fiscal crisis caused by wars and extravagant spending, the spread of Enlightenment ideas of liberty and equality, and contingent political events of 1789. The Third Estate’s demand for voting by head rather than by estate led to the formation of the National Assembly and the subsequent revolutionary cascade. The Revolution transformed France and influenced political thought worldwide.

flashcard.front: What were the Three Estates in pre-revolutionary France and which one paid most of the taxes?
flashcard.back: First Estate – Clergy; Second Estate – Nobility; Third Estate – Commoners. The Third Estate bore almost the entire tax burden.
flashcard.hint: Social structure of the Ancien Régime.
