subject: AP US Government and Politics
title: Enumerated, Reserved, and Concurrent Powers
formulaOrRule: Enumerated powers: delegated to the national government. Reserved powers: retained by states or the people. Concurrent powers: shared by national and state governments. Supremacy Clause: valid federal law prevails over conflicting state law.

variablesOrTerms.Enumerated powers: Powers expressly granted to Congress and the national government, including taxation, regulating interstate commerce, and declaring war.
variablesOrTerms.Reserved powers: Powers not delegated to the national government or prohibited to states, protected by the Tenth Amendment.
variablesOrTerms.Concurrent powers: Powers exercised by both levels of government, such as taxation and borrowing.
variablesOrTerms.Supremacy Clause: Article VI establishes the Constitution and valid federal laws and treaties as the supreme law of the land.
variablesOrTerms.Necessary and Proper Clause: Article I, Section 8 permits Congress to enact laws necessary and proper for carrying out its enumerated powers.
variablesOrTerms.Federalism: The constitutional division of governing authority between national and state governments.

derivationOrExplanation: The Constitution assigns certain powers directly to the national government while leaving other powers to states or the people. Some responsibilities overlap, creating concurrent powers. The Necessary and Proper Clause gives Congress flexibility to implement its enumerated responsibilities through implied powers. The Supremacy Clause resolves conflicts when valid federal law and state law cannot coexist. Federal supremacy does not mean every federal action automatically overrides state authority: the federal action must be constitutionally valid. The Tenth Amendment reinforces the principle that powers not delegated to the United States and not prohibited to the states are reserved.

flashcard.front: What happens when valid federal law conflicts with state law?
flashcard.back: The Supremacy Clause makes valid federal law controlling.

subject: AP US Government and Politics
title: Federalist No. 10 Versus Federalist No. 51
formulaOrRule: Federalist No. 10: control the effects of factions through an extended republic. Federalist No. 51: control government power through separation of powers and checks and balances.

variablesOrTerms.Faction: A group of citizens united by a common interest or passion that may conflict with others' rights or the public good.
variablesOrTerms.Extended republic: A large republic with many competing interests, making it harder for one faction to dominate.
variablesOrTerms.Pluralism: Competition among multiple groups seeking to influence public policy.
variablesOrTerms.Separation of powers: Division of government authority among legislative, executive, and judicial branches.
variablesOrTerms.Checks and balances: Constitutional mechanisms allowing each branch to limit the powers of the others.
variablesOrTerms.Ambition counteracting ambition: Madison's argument that institutional self-interest can help prevent one branch from becoming dominant.

derivationOrExplanation: In Federalist No. 10, James Madison argues that factions are unavoidable because people have different interests and unequal property. Rather than eliminating their causes, a large republic can limit their harmful effects by multiplying competing interests and making majority domination more difficult. In Federalist No. 51, Madison focuses on preventing government tyranny. Dividing power among branches and giving each branch constitutional means to resist encroachment creates institutional checks. The first essay emphasizes controlling factions in society; the second emphasizes controlling power within government.

flashcard.front: What is the central difference between Federalist 10 and 51?
flashcard.back: No. 10 controls factions; No. 51 checks government power.

subject: AP US Government and Politics
title: Key Amendments: Civil Liberties, Rights, and Equality
formulaOrRule: First Amendment: expression and religion. Fourth: searches and seizures. Fifth: due process and protections for the accused. Sixth: criminal trial rights. Thirteenth: abolishes slavery. Fourteenth: citizenship, due process, and equal protection. Fifteenth: voting rights regardless of race. Nineteenth: voting rights regardless of sex.

variablesOrTerms.First Amendment: Protects religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition.
variablesOrTerms.Fourth Amendment: Protects against unreasonable searches and seizures; warrants generally require probable cause.
variablesOrTerms.Fifth Amendment: Includes grand jury protections in federal cases, protection against double jeopardy and compelled self-incrimination, due process, and takings compensation.
variablesOrTerms.Sixth Amendment: Guarantees speedy and public trial, impartial jury, notice of charges, confrontation, compulsory process, and assistance of counsel in criminal prosecutions.
variablesOrTerms.Thirteenth Amendment: Abolishes slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment for a crime after conviction.
variablesOrTerms.Fourteenth Amendment: Establishes national citizenship and includes Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses.
variablesOrTerms.Fifteenth Amendment: Prohibits denying voting rights on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
variablesOrTerms.Nineteenth Amendment: Prohibits denying voting rights on account of sex.

derivationOrExplanation: These amendments expand constitutional protections and define limits on government authority. The First, Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Amendments protect important liberties and procedural rights. The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery, while the Fourteenth established citizenship and constitutional protections that became central to applying many Bill of Rights protections against state governments through selective incorporation. The Fifteenth and Nineteenth Amendments prohibit specific forms of voting discrimination. Remember that the Fifteenth Amendment does not itself prohibit every possible voting restriction; later laws and constitutional interpretations address additional barriers.

flashcard.front: Which amendment contains the Equal Protection Clause?
flashcard.back: The Fourteenth Amendment.

subject: AP Macroeconomics
topic: Production possibilities curve and economic growth
title: PPC Opportunity Cost and Economic Growth
formulaOrRule: Opportunity cost = quantity of the alternative good sacrificed / additional quantity of the chosen good. Economic growth shifts the PPC outward.

variablesOrTerms.Production Possibilities Curve (PPC): A curve showing the maximum attainable combinations of two goods with current resources and technology.
variablesOrTerms.Opportunity cost: The next-best alternative sacrificed when making a choice.
variablesOrTerms.Economic growth: An increase in productive capacity caused by more or better resources or improved technology.

derivationOrExplanation: Moving along a PPC illustrates trade-offs: producing more of one good requires sacrificing some of the other. With a bowed-out PPC, opportunity cost generally increases as production shifts toward one good because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods. A point inside the curve indicates underused resources or inefficiency, while a point on the curve represents productive efficiency. An outward shift indicates increased productive capacity, which can result from technological progress, investment in capital, education, or growth in the labor force. A movement from an inefficient point toward the existing frontier is not itself economic growth.

flashcard.front: What causes an outward shift of the PPC?
flashcard.back: More or better resources, or improved production technology.

subject: AP Microeconomics
topic: Price controls and excise tax incidence
title: Price Ceilings, Price Floors, and Tax Incidence
formulaOrRule: Binding price ceiling: below equilibrium, causing shortage. Binding price floor: above equilibrium, causing surplus. The relatively less elastic side of a market bears more of an excise tax burden.

variablesOrTerms.Price ceiling: A legal maximum price; binding when set below equilibrium.
variablesOrTerms.Price floor: A legal minimum price; binding when set above equilibrium.
variablesOrTerms.Excise tax: A per-unit tax imposed on the sale or production of a good.
variablesOrTerms.Tax incidence: The distribution of the economic burden of a tax between buyers and sellers.
variablesOrTerms.Elasticity: A measure of how responsive quantity demanded or supplied is to a change in price.

derivationOrExplanation: A binding ceiling prevents the market price from rising to equilibrium, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. A binding floor prevents the price from falling to equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. An excise tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive, reducing the quantity traded. Statutory responsibility for paying the tax does not determine who bears its economic burden. The less elastic side has fewer opportunities to adjust quantity and therefore bears a larger share of the burden. If demand is relatively inelastic, consumers generally bear more; if supply is relatively inelastic, producers generally bear more.

flashcard.front: Who bears more of an excise tax burden?
flashcard.back: The relatively less elastic side of the market.

title: Monopoly Deadweight Loss and Price Discrimination
formulaOrRule: A single-price monopoly chooses output where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve at that output. Deadweight loss results when monopoly output is below the allocatively efficient quantity where P = MC.

variablesOrTerms.Marginal revenue (MR): The additional revenue from selling one more unit.
variablesOrTerms.Marginal cost (MC): The additional cost of producing one more unit.
variablesOrTerms.Demand curve: Shows the maximum willingness to pay for each quantity.
variablesOrTerms.Deadweight loss: The loss of total surplus from mutually beneficial trades that do not occur.
variablesOrTerms.Price discrimination: Charging different prices to different consumers for the same good or service when price differences are not explained by cost differences.
variablesOrTerms.First-degree price discrimination: Charging each buyer their maximum willingness to pay for each unit.
variablesOrTerms.Market power: A firm's ability to influence the market price.

derivationOrExplanation: A single-price monopolist maximizes profit by producing the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, then charging the highest price consumers will pay for that quantity according to the demand curve. Because the monopoly restricts output below the competitive or allocatively efficient level, some trades for which willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost do not occur, creating deadweight loss. Price discrimination can increase monopoly profit when the firm has market power, can identify or separate buyers by willingness to pay, and can prevent resale or arbitrage. Perfect first-degree price discrimination captures consumer surplus and can expand output to the efficient level under standard assumptions, eliminating the usual monopoly deadweight loss.

flashcard.front: What conditions help a firm price discriminate?
flashcard.back: Market power, identifiable buyer differences, and limited resale.

subject: AP Macroeconomics
title: Loanable Funds Market and Real Interest Rates
formulaOrRule: Real interest rate ≈ Nominal interest rate − Inflation rate. In the loanable funds market, saving supplies funds and borrowing for investment and other uses demands funds.

variablesOrTerms.Loanable funds: Funds available for borrowing and lending in financial markets.
variablesOrTerms.Supply of loanable funds: Primarily determined by national saving in the simplified AP model.
variablesOrTerms.Demand for loanable funds: Reflects borrowing for investment and other financing needs.
variablesOrTerms.Nominal interest rate: The stated interest rate measured in money terms.
variablesOrTerms.Real interest rate: The nominal interest rate adjusted for inflation.
variablesOrTerms.Crowding out: A reduction in private investment that can occur when government borrowing raises the real interest rate.

derivationOrExplanation: The loanable funds market determines the equilibrium real interest rate through the interaction of saving and borrowing. An increase in saving shifts supply right and tends to lower the real interest rate while increasing the quantity of funds exchanged. An increase in borrowing demand shifts demand right and tends to raise the real interest rate. A larger government budget deficit can increase government borrowing and, in the standard model, shift demand for loanable funds right, potentially crowding out some private investment. The exact Fisher relationship is (1 + nominal rate) = (1 + real rate)(1 + inflation rate); subtracting inflation from the nominal rate is the common approximation for moderate rates.

flashcard.front: How is the approximate real interest rate calculated?
flashcard.back: Nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate.

subject: AP Macroeconomics
title: Short-Run and Long-Run Phillips Curve Trade-Offs
formulaOrRule: Short run: unexpected changes in aggregate demand can create an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment along the SRPC. Long run: the LRPC is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.

variablesOrTerms.Short-run Phillips Curve (SRPC): A downward-sloping curve showing an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment in the short run.
variablesOrTerms.Long-run Phillips Curve (LRPC): A vertical curve at the natural rate of unemployment.
variablesOrTerms.Natural rate of unemployment: The unemployment rate associated with normal frictional and structural unemployment when cyclical unemployment is zero.
variablesOrTerms.Expected inflation: The inflation rate households and firms anticipate.
variablesOrTerms.Supply shock: An event that changes production costs or aggregate supply, potentially shifting the SRPC.
variablesOrTerms.Stagflation: A combination of high inflation and high unemployment.

derivationOrExplanation: In the short run, stronger aggregate demand can raise output and employment while increasing inflation, moving the economy along a given SRPC. Weaker aggregate demand can lower inflation while increasing unemployment. This trade-off is not permanent. As expectations adjust, workers and firms revise wage and price decisions, shifting the SRPC. In the long run, unemployment returns to its natural rate regardless of the inflation rate, so the LRPC is vertical. Adverse supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment simultaneously, shifting the SRPC in an unfavorable direction and producing stagflation.

flashcard.front: Why is the long-run Phillips curve vertical?
flashcard.back: Unemployment returns to its natural rate regardless of long-run inflation.

subject: AP Macroeconomics
topic: Loanable funds and fiscal policy transmission
title: Government Deficits and Crowding Out
formulaOrRule: Budget deficit increases government borrowing → demand for loanable funds shifts right → real interest rate rises → private investment may fall.

variablesOrTerms.Budget deficit: A situation in which government spending exceeds government revenue during a period.
variablesOrTerms.Government borrowing: The financing of a deficit through issuing debt.
variablesOrTerms.Demand for loanable funds: Borrowing demand from government and private borrowers in the simplified market model.
variablesOrTerms.Private investment: Business spending on capital goods and other productive investment.
variablesOrTerms.Crowding out: The decline in private investment associated with higher interest rates caused by government borrowing.

derivationOrExplanation: When the government runs a larger deficit and finances it by borrowing, demand for loanable funds can increase. With the supply of loanable funds unchanged, the equilibrium real interest rate rises. Higher borrowing costs can discourage businesses from financing capital projects, reducing private investment. This is called crowding out. The extent depends on conditions in financial markets and the economy; it is not necessarily complete. In a recession with substantial unused resources, crowding out may be smaller than when the economy is near full employment.

flashcard.front: What is the standard crowding-out mechanism?
flashcard.back: Government borrowing raises real rates and may reduce private investment.

subject: AP Psychology
topic: Biological bases of behavior and neural communication
title: Action Potential and Neural Impulse
formulaOrRule: Resting potential → threshold → depolarization → repolarization → hyperpolarization → return to resting potential. An action potential is an all-or-none electrical impulse.

variablesOrTerms.Resting potential: The neuron's usual negative internal charge relative to the outside, commonly around −70 mV.
variablesOrTerms.Threshold: The membrane voltage that triggers an action potential.
variablesOrTerms.Depolarization: Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions enter the neuron.
variablesOrTerms.Repolarization: Voltage-gated potassium channels open and potassium ions leave the neuron.
variablesOrTerms.Hyperpolarization: A brief period when the membrane becomes more negative than its resting potential.
variablesOrTerms.Refractory period: A period when another action potential cannot or is less likely to occur.
variablesOrTerms.All-or-none principle: Once threshold is reached, the action potential occurs at a consistent amplitude.

derivationOrExplanation: A neuron maintains a resting membrane potential through ion concentration gradients and selective membrane permeability. When stimulation brings the membrane to threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, allowing sodium to enter and rapidly depolarize the membrane. Sodium channels then inactivate while potassium channels open, allowing potassium to leave and repolarize the membrane. Potassium channels may remain open briefly, producing hyperpolarization. The membrane then returns toward its resting state. Stronger stimulation does not make an individual action potential larger; it can increase the frequency of action potentials.

flashcard.front: Which ion enters during neuronal depolarization?
flashcard.back: Sodium ions (Na⁺).

subject: AP Psychology
title: Synaptic Transmission and Reuptake
formulaOrRule: Action potential reaches axon terminal → neurotransmitter release → receptor binding → postsynaptic response → neurotransmitter removal or reuptake.

variablesOrTerms.Synapse: The junction where a neuron communicates with another cell.
variablesOrTerms.Axon terminal: The end of an axon where neurotransmitters are released.
variablesOrTerms.Neurotransmitter: A chemical messenger that transmits signals across a synapse.
variablesOrTerms.Synaptic cleft: The small gap between communicating cells.
variablesOrTerms.Receptor: A protein that binds a particular neurotransmitter and influences the receiving cell.
variablesOrTerms.Reuptake: The reabsorption of neurotransmitters into the presynaptic neuron.
variablesOrTerms.Enzymatic breakdown: The chemical breakdown of neurotransmitters by enzymes in or near the synapse.

derivationOrExplanation: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters from synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft. These chemicals bind to compatible receptors on the postsynaptic cell and can produce excitatory or inhibitory effects. Their action is terminated through mechanisms such as reuptake into the sending neuron, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion away from the synapse. Reuptake inhibitors increase the time certain neurotransmitters remain available in the synaptic cleft. Neurotransmitter effects depend on the receptor and neural pathway, not simply on the chemical's name.

flashcard.front: What is neurotransmitter reuptake?
flashcard.back: The presynaptic neuron reabsorbs released neurotransmitters.

subject: AP Psychology
title: Bottom-Up, Top-Down, and Gestalt Processing
formulaOrRule: Bottom-up processing: sensory input → perception. Top-down processing: expectations and prior knowledge → interpretation of sensory input.

variablesOrTerms.Bottom-up processing: Perception built from incoming sensory information.
variablesOrTerms.Top-down processing: Perception influenced by expectations, experience, and prior knowledge.
variablesOrTerms.Gestalt psychology: An approach emphasizing how the mind organizes sensory information into meaningful wholes.
variablesOrTerms.Proximity: Objects close together tend to be perceived as belonging to a group.
variablesOrTerms.Similarity: Similar objects tend to be grouped together.
variablesOrTerms.Closure: The mind tends to fill gaps to perceive complete forms.
variablesOrTerms.Continuity: The mind tends to perceive smooth, continuous patterns rather than abrupt changes.

derivationOrExplanation: Bottom-up processing begins with the features detected by sensory receptors and builds toward recognition. Top-down processing uses context, expectations, and knowledge to interpret ambiguous or incomplete input. Both processes commonly work together. Gestalt principles describe how the perceptual system organizes separate elements into patterns. For example, a group of similar symbols may be perceived as one category, while nearby objects may be seen as belonging together. Closure explains why people often perceive a complete shape even when parts of its outline are missing.

flashcard.front: How do bottom-up and top-down processing differ?
flashcard.back: Bottom-up starts with sensory input; top-down uses expectations and knowledge.

subject: AP Psychology
title: Atkinson-Shiffrin and Baddeley Memory Models
formulaOrRule: Atkinson-Shiffrin: sensory memory → short-term memory → long-term memory. Baddeley: working memory coordinates temporary storage and processing through specialized components.

variablesOrTerms.Sensory memory: A brief initial record of sensory information.
variablesOrTerms.Short-term memory: A limited-capacity system that temporarily holds information.
variablesOrTerms.Long-term memory: A relatively enduring store of information.
variablesOrTerms.Working memory: An active system for temporarily holding and manipulating information.
variablesOrTerms.Central executive: Directs attention and coordinates working-memory processes.
variablesOrTerms.Phonological loop: Temporarily holds and rehearses speech-based and auditory information.
variablesOrTerms.Visuospatial sketchpad: Temporarily holds and manipulates visual and spatial information.
variablesOrTerms.Episodic buffer: Integrates information from different sources into a unified representation.
variablesOrTerms.Explicit memory: Conscious memory for facts and experiences, including semantic and episodic memory.
variablesOrTerms.Implicit memory: Memory expressed through performance or behavior, including procedural memory.

derivationOrExplanation: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model describes memory as a flow from sensory registration to short-term storage and then long-term storage, with attention and rehearsal influencing transfer. Baddeley's working-memory model provides a more detailed account of active short-term processing. Its central executive coordinates the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and episodic buffer. Long-term memory can be divided into explicit memory, which includes semantic facts and episodic experiences, and implicit memory, which includes skills and habits. These models describe complementary aspects of memory rather than mutually exclusive explanations.

flashcard.front: Which working-memory component handles verbal information?
flashcard.back: The phonological loop.

subject: AP Psychology
title: Cognitive Heuristics and Confirmation Bias
formulaOrRule: Availability: judge likelihood by ease of recall. Representativeness: judge likelihood by similarity to a prototype. Anchoring: rely heavily on an initial value. Confirmation bias: favor information supporting existing beliefs.

variablesOrTerms.Heuristic: A mental shortcut that can make judgment faster but may produce systematic errors.
variablesOrTerms.Availability heuristic: Estimating frequency or probability based on how easily examples come to mind.
variablesOrTerms.Representativeness heuristic: Judging likelihood by resemblance to a category or prototype.
variablesOrTerms.Anchoring bias: Relying excessively on an initial piece of information when making judgments.
variablesOrTerms.Confirmation bias: Seeking, interpreting, or remembering information in ways that support existing beliefs.
variablesOrTerms.Cognitive bias: A systematic pattern of deviation from fully rational judgment.

derivationOrExplanation: Heuristics simplify complex decisions but can lead to predictable errors. After seeing dramatic news coverage of an unusual event, a person may overestimate how frequently it occurs because examples are easy to recall; this is availability. Assuming someone belongs to a profession because they resemble a stereotype illustrates representativeness. An initial price can influence later estimates even when it is arbitrary, illustrating anchoring. Confirmation bias occurs when a person gives greater attention to evidence supporting an existing belief while discounting contradictory information. These processes can operate together but describe different mechanisms.

flashcard.front: Which heuristic relies on how easily examples come to mind?
flashcard.back: The availability heuristic.

subject: AP Psychology
title: Validity, Reliability, and Experimental Controls
formulaOrRule: Reliability = consistency of measurement. Validity = whether a measure or study assesses what it is intended to assess. Strong experiments use operational definitions, control groups, and appropriate controls for bias.

variablesOrTerms.Reliability: The consistency or repeatability of a measurement.
variablesOrTerms.Validity: The extent to which a measurement or study supports the intended interpretation.
variablesOrTerms.Operational definition: A precise description of how a variable is measured or manipulated.
variablesOrTerms.Control group: A comparison group that does not receive the experimental treatment or receives a standard condition.
variablesOrTerms.Placebo: An inactive treatment designed to resemble the experimental treatment.
variablesOrTerms.Double-blind procedure: Neither participants nor the researchers interacting with them know who receives the treatment during the study.
variablesOrTerms.Confounding variable: An uncontrolled factor that varies with the independent variable and could affect the outcome.
variablesOrTerms.Random assignment: Assigning participants to conditions by chance to help distribute preexisting differences.

derivationOrExplanation: A reliable measure produces consistent results across repeated uses, but consistency alone does not guarantee validity. A scale that always adds five kilograms is reliable in a narrow sense but inaccurate. Validity concerns whether the measure supports the intended conclusion. Operational definitions make variables observable and measurable. A placebo control helps separate treatment effects from expectations, while double-blind procedures reduce expectancy effects and researcher bias. Random assignment helps make experimental groups comparable. Researchers should also control confounding variables and use ethical procedures, informed consent, and appropriate participant protections.

flashcard.front: How does reliability differ from validity?
flashcard.back: Reliability is consistency; validity is measuring what is intended.

subject: AP World History
title: Corroborating Evidence Across Historical Documents
formulaOrRule: Corroboration = comparing independent sources to identify agreement, disagreement, and differences in perspective; use sourcing analysis to explain why those differences matter.

variablesOrTerms.Corroboration: Comparing multiple sources to assess whether they support, complicate, or contradict an interpretation.
variablesOrTerms.Agreement: A point on which multiple sources provide consistent evidence.
variablesOrTerms.Contradiction: A difference between sources that may reflect perspective, purpose, access to information, or context.
variablesOrTerms.Perspective: The position or viewpoint from which a source presents an event.
variablesOrTerms.Reliability: The degree to which a source is useful for a particular historical question, considering its origin and purpose.

derivationOrExplanation: Historians do not assume that one document provides a complete account of an event. They compare sources created by different people, institutions, or groups. If two accounts agree on a detail, that agreement may strengthen an interpretation, especially when the sources are independent. If they disagree, examine each author's historical situation, audience, purpose, and point of view. A government report may emphasize official success, while a local account may describe disruption or resistance. Rather than automatically treating one source as true and the other as false, explain how their different positions shape the evidence and what can reasonably be concluded.

flashcard.front: What does corroboration help historians evaluate?
flashcard.back: Whether multiple sources support, complicate, or contradict an interpretation.

title: Mean Value Theorem and Extreme Value Theorem
formulaOrRule: MVT: If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists c with f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}. EVT: A continuous function on a closed interval [a,b] attains an absolute maximum and minimum.
derivationOrExplanation: The MVT guarantees a point where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope. The EVT guarantees existence of absolute extrema on a closed, bounded interval for a continuous function.

title: Ratio Test and Alternating Series Test
formulaOrRule: Ratio Test: L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|; converges absolutely if L<1, diverges if L>1. Alternating Series Test: if a_n>0, decreasing, and \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=0, then \sum(-1)^na_n converges.

title: Safe Removal Patterns for ArrayLists

title: Recursion Call Stack and Base Cases

formulaOrRule: $y = mx + b$

variablesOrTerms.m: slope; rise over run; rate of change (unitless ratio)

derivationOrExplanation: Rearranging any linear equation $Ax + By = C$ into $y = mx + b$ isolates the slope and intercept for direct reading. Common Digital SAT trap: the y-intercept is the point $(0, b)$, not just the number $b$ when asked for a coordinate; also watch for sign errors when $b$ is negative.

flashcard.back: Rewrite as $y = -3x + 4$; slope = −3, y-intercept = 4 (point (0, 4)).

subject: SAT Math
topic: Advanced Math > Quadratic Equations > Quadratic Formula
title: Quadratic Formula
formulaOrRule: $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$

variablesOrTerms.±: indicates two solutions, one with + and one with −

derivationOrExplanation: The formula comes from completing the square on the general quadratic $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$. Example: for $2x^2 - 4x - 6 = 0$, substitute a = 2, b = −4, c = −6 to get $x = (4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 48})/4 = (4 \pm 8)/4$, giving x = 3 or x = −1. Digital SAT trap: sign errors when b is negative inside the formula (the leading $-b$ becomes positive) and forgetting the ± yields only one root.

flashcard.hint: List a, b, c with signs first; the discriminant is 16.

subject: SAT Math
title: Point-Slope Form

variablesOrTerms.(x₁, y₁): a known point on the line
variablesOrTerms.(x, y): any other point on the line

derivationOrExplanation: This form comes directly from the slope definition $m = (y - y_1)/(x - x_1)$ multiplied through by $(x - x_1)$. Example: a line through (2, −1) with slope 4 is $y + 1 = 4(x - 2)$. Digital SAT trap: the signs flip inside the parentheses, so a point (−3, 5) produces $(x + 3)$ and $(y - 5)$, not $(x - 3)$ and $(y + 5)$.

flashcard.front: Write the point-slope equation for a line through (−3, 5) with slope −2.
flashcard.hint: Minus a negative becomes plus; match signs carefully.

subject: SAT Math
topic: Algebra > Linear Equations > Parallel and Perpendicular Slopes
title: Parallel and Perpendicular Slope Conditions
formulaOrRule: Parallel: $m_1 = m_2$; Perpendicular: $m_1 m_2 = -1$

variablesOrTerms.negative reciprocal: flip the fraction and change the sign; e.g., 2/3 → −3/2

derivationOrExplanation: Parallel lines never intersect, so they rise at the same rate and share slope. Perpendicular lines meet at 90°, and rotating a slope vector 90° produces the negative reciprocal, giving $m_1 m_2 = -1$. Example: a line perpendicular to $y = \frac{2}{3}x + 1$ has slope $-\frac{3}{2}$. Trap: horizontal lines (slope 0) are perpendicular to vertical lines (undefined slope), which cannot be captured by the product rule.

flashcard.front: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to $y = -\frac{4}{5}x + 7$?
flashcard.back: $m = \frac{5}{4}$ (negative reciprocal of −4/5).
flashcard.hint: Flip and flip the sign; product of slopes must equal −1.

subject: SAT Math
topic: Algebra > Systems of Two Linear Equations > Number of Solutions
title: No-Solution and Infinite-Solution Conditions
formulaOrRule: No solution: $\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \frac{c_1}{c_2}$; Infinite: $\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{c_1}{c_2}$

variablesOrTerms.a₁x + b₁y = c₁: first linear equation in standard form
variablesOrTerms.ratio equality: all three ratios equal means same line; first two equal but third different means parallel distinct lines

derivationOrExplanation: Two lines have no solution when they are parallel (same slope, different intercept), and infinitely many when they are the same line. In standard form, slope is $-a/b$ and intercept is $c/b$, so comparing ratios captures both conditions at once. Example: $2x + 3y = 6$ and $4x + 6y = 10$ have no solution (ratios 1/2, 1/2, 3/5). Trap: on the SAT, a parameter like $k$ often appears and you must set ratios equal or unequal accordingly; double-check whether the constant ratio matches.

flashcard.front: For what value of $k$ does the system $kx + 4y = 8$ and $3x + 6y = 12$ have infinitely many solutions?
flashcard.back: $k = 2$ (all ratios equal: k/3 = 4/6 = 8/12 = 2/3).
flashcard.hint: Cross-multiply corresponding coefficients; all three must match.

topic: Algebra > Linear Inequalities in One or Two Variables
title: Solving Linear Inequalities
formulaOrRule: If $a < b$, then $a + c < b + c$; if $c < 0$, then $ac > bc$ (flip sign)

variablesOrTerms.flip rule: multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality direction
variablesOrTerms.solution set: all values satisfying the inequality; graphed as half-plane (two variables) or interval (one variable)

derivationOrExplanation: Inequalities behave like equations except when multiplying or dividing by a negative number, which reverses order because the number line reflects. Example: $-2x + 5 > 11$ becomes $-2x > 6$, then $x < -3$. Digital SAT trap: forgetting to flip when dividing by a negative; also, for two-variable inequalities, a dashed boundary means strict (<, >) and a solid boundary means inclusive (≤, ≥), with shading toward the test-point side.

flashcard.front: Solve $-3x + 7 \leq 22$.
flashcard.back: $x \geq -5$ (subtract 7, divide by −3 and flip the sign).

subject: SAT Math
title: Discriminant and Number of Real Roots
formulaOrRule: $D = b^2 - 4ac$; $D > 0$: two real roots; $D = 0$: one real root; $D < 0$: no real roots

variablesOrTerms.D: discriminant, the expression under the square root in the quadratic formula
variablesOrTerms.one real root: parabola is tangent to x-axis (double root)

derivationOrExplanation: The discriminant is the radicand $b^2 - 4ac$ from the quadratic formula; its sign determines whether the square root is real, zero, or imaginary. Example: $x^2 + 4x + 4$ has $D = 16 - 16 = 0$, so it has exactly one real root (x = −2). Digital SAT trap: questions ask for the number of real solutions, not complex ones, and sometimes ask for the value of a parameter that makes $D = 0$; set the discriminant equal to zero and solve.

flashcard.front: How many real solutions does $2x^2 - 3x + 5 = 0$ have?
flashcard.hint: Compute $b^2 - 4ac$ mentally before choosing a method.

subject: SAT Math
topic: Advanced Math > Quadratic Functions > Vertex Form
title: Vertex Form of a Parabola

variablesOrTerms.a: vertical stretch/compression factor; opens up if a > 0, down if a < 0
variablesOrTerms.h: x-coordinate of vertex; axis of symmetry is x = h
variablesOrTerms.k: minimum (a > 0) or maximum (a < 0) value of the function

derivationOrExplanation: Vertex form is obtained by completing the square on $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, producing $a(x - h)^2 + k$ with $h = -b/(2a)$ and $k = c - b^2/(4a)$. Example: $y = x^2 - 6x + 11$ becomes $y = (x - 3)^2 + 2$, vertex (3, 2), minimum value 2. Digital SAT trap: the sign of h flips—$(x - 3)^2$ means h = 3, not −3; also, the minimum/maximum is the k-value, not the vertex point unless asked for coordinates.

flashcard.front: What is the vertex of $y = 2(x + 4)^2 - 7$?
flashcard.back: (−4, −7); the minimum value is −7.
flashcard.hint: Inside parentheses: sign flips. Outside: sign stays.

subject: SAT Math
topic: Advanced Math > Quadratic Equations > Sum and Product of Roots
title: Vieta's Formulas
formulaOrRule: Sum of roots $= -\frac{b}{a}$; Product of roots $= \frac{c}{a}$

variablesOrTerms.roots: solutions r₁ and r₂ of the quadratic equation

derivationOrExplanation: If $ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - r_1)(x - r_2)$, expanding gives $a[x^2 - (r_1 + r_2)x + r_1 r_2]$, so $b = -a(r_1 + r_2)$ and $c = a r_1 r_2$. Example: $2x^2 - 8x + 6 = 0$ has sum $8/2 = 4$ and product $6/2 = 3$. Digital SAT trap: the sum formula has a negative sign that is easy to drop; double-check whether the equation is in standard form with a ≠ 1 before applying ratios.

flashcard.front: For $3x^2 - 12x + 7 = 0$, find the sum and product of the roots.
flashcard.back: Sum = 4; product = 7/3.
flashcard.hint: Sum = −b/a, product = c/a; keep signs attached to b and c.

title: Exponential Growth/Decay Model
formulaOrRule: $y = a(1 \pm r)^t$

variablesOrTerms.r: growth rate (use +) or decay rate (use −), as a decimal
variablesOrTerms.1 ± r: growth/decay factor; e.g., 1.05 means 5% growth per period

derivationOrExplanation: Each period multiplies the previous amount by the same factor $(1 \pm r)$, so repeated multiplication yields the exponent t. Example: $200 invested at 4% annual growth is $200(1.04)^t$. Digital SAT trap: the rate must be converted to a decimal (4% → 0.04), and if compounding occurs more than once per year, divide r by the number of periods and multiply t accordingly; also, decay factor 0.85 means 15% decrease, not 85%.

flashcard.hint: Decay factor = 1 − 0.12 = 0.88; square it for 2 years.

title: Compound Interest Formula
formulaOrRule: $A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}$

variablesOrTerms.r: annual interest rate as a decimal

derivationOrExplanation: Compounding n times per year divides the annual rate by n and applies the growth factor nt times, generalizing $y = a(1 + r)^t$. title: Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem
formulaOrRule: Remainder of $P(x) \div (x - c)$ is $P(c)$; $(x - c)$ is a factor iff $P(c) = 0$

variablesOrTerms.P(c): value of polynomial at x = c; equals the remainder
variablesOrTerms.factor: a polynomial that divides evenly with zero remainder

derivationOrExplanation: Dividing $P(x)$ by $(x - c)$ gives $P(x) = (x - c)Q(x) + R$; substituting x = c eliminates the first term, leaving $P(c) = R$. Example: dividing $x^3 - 2x + 4$ by $(x - 1)$ gives remainder $P(1) = 1 - 2 + 4 = 3$. Digital SAT trap: the divisor $(x + 3)$ corresponds to c = −3, not 3; substitute the value that makes the divisor zero.

flashcard.hint: Set divisor = 0 to find c; evaluate directly, no long division.

subject: SAT Math
title: Vertical and Horizontal Asymptotes of Rational Functions
formulaOrRule: Vertical: denominator = 0 (after canceling common factors); Horizontal: compare degrees of numerator $n$ and denominator $m$ ($n < m \implies y = 0$; $n = m \implies y = a/b$; $n > m \implies$ none)

variablesOrTerms.vertical asymptote: x-value where function is undefined and approaches $\pm\infty$; set reduced denominator = 0
variablesOrTerms.horizontal asymptote: end behavior as $x \to \pm\infty$; if $n < m$ then $y = 0$; if $n = m$ then $y = a/b$; if $n > m$ no horizontal asymptote
variablesOrTerms.a, b: leading coefficients of numerator and denominator when degrees are equal

derivationOrExplanation: For a rational function $f(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$, cancel any common factors first (common factors produce removable discontinuities or holes, not vertical asymptotes). Vertical asymptotes occur at values of $x$ where the reduced denominator equals zero. For horizontal asymptotes, evaluate the limit as $x \to \pm\infty$: if the degree of the numerator $n < m$, the denominator dominates so $y = 0$; if $n = m$, the highest-degree terms dominate yielding $y = \frac{a}{b}$; if $n > m$, the values grow without bound and there is no horizontal asymptote (or a slant asymptote if $n = m + 1$).

flashcard.front: How do you find the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of a rational function $f(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$?
flashcard.back: Vertical: simplify $f(x)$ and solve reduced denominator $= 0$. Horizontal: if degrees $n < m$, $y = 0$; if $n = m$, $y = a/b$; if $n > m$, none.
flashcard.hint: Check for common factors (holes) first, then compare numerator and denominator degrees.

By calculus definition: a = dv/dt => ∫dv = ∫a dt => v = u + at. Substituting v = ds/dt and integrating yields s = ut + 0.5at². Eliminating t yields v² = u² + 2as. Evaluating s(n) - s(n-1) gives s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1).

subject: Physics
title: Dynamics: Work-Energy Theorem & Centripetal Acceleration
formulaOrRule:
Work-Energy Theorem & Instantaneous Power: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_i^2, \quad P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$;
Centripetal Acceleration & Safe Banking Speed: $a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r, \quad v_{\text{safe}} = \sqrt{r g \left(\frac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}\right)}$

variablesOrTerms.W_net: Net work executed on object by all forces combined (Joules, J)
variablesOrTerms.\\mu_s: Static friction coefficient between tires and road
variablesOrTerms.\\theta: Road banking angle with horizontal plane (°)

derivationOrExplanation:
W = ∫ F dx = ∫ m (dv/dt) dx = ∫ m v dv = [0.5 m v²] from v_i to v_f = ΔK. Instantaneous power P = dW/dt = F · (dx/dt) = F · v.
Drill: A 1200 kg vehicle accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s. Compute net work done and required engine power if this occurs in 5 seconds.

In circular path of radius r, velocity direction rotates by Δθ in time Δt, producing radial acceleration limit v²/r. On banked road, balancing horizontal centripetal requirement N sin θ + f cos θ = m v²/r with vertical normal N cos θ - f sin θ = mg yields maximum banking velocity.
Drill: A highway curve has radius 150 m banked at 15° with friction coefficient 0.2. Calculate the maximum safe non-skid speed (g = 9.8 m/s²).

subject: Physics
title: Gravitation: Escape Velocity & Simple Harmonic Oscillations
formulaOrRule:
Escape Velocity & Orbital Velocity: $v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}, \quad v_o = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R}} = \frac{v_e}{\sqrt{2}}$;
Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) Period & Energy: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \quad E_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2$

variablesOrTerms.v_o: Orbital speed for satellite in near-surface orbit (m/s)
variablesOrTerms.A: Oscillation amplitude: max displacement from mean equilibrium (m)
variablesOrTerms.E_total: Total mechanical energy of oscillating system (J)

derivationOrExplanation:
By energy conservation, total energy at surface must be >= 0 to reach infinity: (1/2)m v_e² - GMm/R = 0 => v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR). For circular orbit, gravitational pull provides centripetal force: GMm/R² = m v_o²/R => v_o = √(GM/R) = v_e / √2.
Drill: Given Earth radius 6,400 km and g = 9.8 m/s², calculate Earth's escape velocity and circular orbital velocity in km/s.

Equation of motion: m(d²x/dt²) = -kx => d²x/dt² + (k/m)x = 0. Angular frequency ω = √(k/m). Time period T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k). Kinetic energy K = (1/2)m v² and Potential energy U = (1/2)k x². Sum K + U = (1/2)k A².
Drill: A 0.5 kg mass hangs from a vertical spring of stiffness k = 200 N/m. Find its natural oscillation frequency and total energy when amplitude is 0.05 m.

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \quad E_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2$ (Time period of linear harmonic oscillator and total invariant mechanical vibrational energy.)

subject: Chemistry
title: Stoichiometry: Mole Concept, Molarity & Molality
formulaOrRule:
Fundamental Mole Conversions: $n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{N}{N_A} = \frac{V_{\text{STP}}}{22.4\text{ L}} \quad (N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23})$;
Molarity, Molality & Dilution Law: $M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution (L)}}}, \quad m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{W_{\text{solvent (kg)}}}, \quad M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2$

variablesOrTerms.n: Amount of substance in chemical moles (mol)
variablesOrTerms.m: Molality of solution (moles per kilogram of solvent, m or mol/kg)
variablesOrTerms.M: Molarity of solution (moles per litre, M or mol/L)
variablesOrTerms.N: Number of elementary entities (atoms, molecules, or ions)
variablesOrTerms.V_STP: Volume of ideal gas at STP (0°C, 1 atm) in litres (L)
variablesOrTerms.W_solvent: Mass of pure solvent in kilograms (kg)
variablesOrTerms.V_1: Volume of stock solution needed (L or mL)
variablesOrTerms.V_2: Final total diluted volume (L or mL)

derivationOrExplanation:
1 mole is defined as containing exactly 6.022 × 10²³ elementary entities (N_A). Dividing mass by formula weight yields moles; multiplying moles by 22.4 L yields volume of an ideal gas at STP.
Drill: Calculate the number of moles and oxygen molecules present in 11.2 litres of O2 gas at STP.

Molarity is volumetric: moles solute / litres solution. Since volume expands with temperature, M changes with T. Molality uses solvent mass (kg), making it temperature invariant. In dilution, total moles of solute remains constant: n = M1 V1 = M2 V2.
Drill: How many mL of 12.0 M concentrated HCl are required to prepare 500 mL of 0.30 M HCl solution?

flashcard.front: What are the core equations and laws for Stoichiometry: Mole Concept, Molarity & Molality?
flashcard.back:
$n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{N}{N_A} = \frac{V_{\text{STP}}}{22.4\text{ L}} \quad (N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23})$ (Converting mass, entity particle count, and standard gas volume into chemical moles.)
$M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution (L)}}}, \quad m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{W_{\text{solvent (kg)}}}, \quad M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2$ (Volumetric molarity versus temperature-independent molality and volumetric dilution equation.)

subject: Chemistry
title: Physical Chemistry: Bohr Atom, de Broglie & Gibbs Energy
formulaOrRule:
Bohr Energy & de Broglie Wavelength: $E_n = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}, \quad r_n = 0.529 \frac{n^2}{Z} \text{ \AA}, \quad \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}$;
First Law, Enthalpy & Gibbs Free Energy: $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT, \quad \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, \quad \Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K_p$

variablesOrTerms.E_n: Total energy of electron in principal quantum shell n (electron-volts, eV)
variablesOrTerms.r_n: Radius of n-th Bohr electronic orbit (Angstroms, Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m)
variablesOrTerms.Z: Nuclear charge / atomic number of hydrogenic species
variablesOrTerms.\\Delta n_g: Change in moles of gaseous species (n_products - n_reactants)
variablesOrTerms.\\Delta G: Gibbs Free Energy change: criterion for spontaneity at constant T, P (kJ/mol)

derivationOrExplanation:
Bohr quantized angular momentum L = mvr = nh/(2π). Balancing Coulombic attraction with centripetal force yields r_n = n²h²/(4π²mZe²) = 0.529 n²/Z Å. Total energy E = K + U = -13.6 Z²/n² eV. de Broglie unified wave-particle duality: λ = h/p.
Drill: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron (m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s.

By definition H = U + PV. For ideal gases PV = n_g RT, hence at constant T, ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT. Gibbs energy G = H - TS. At constant T, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. At chemical equilibrium ΔG = 0, which yields ΔG° = -RT ln K.
Drill: For a reaction ΔH = -92 kJ/mol and ΔS = -198 J/(mol·K). Determine whether the reaction is spontaneous at 298 K.

flashcard.back:
$E_n = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}, \quad r_n = 0.529 \frac{n^2}{Z} \text{ \AA}, \quad \lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}$ (Quantized electronic stationary state energies, orbital radii, and matter wave wavelength.)
$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT, \quad \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, \quad \Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K_p$ (Thermochemical state functions, spontaneity criterion (ΔG < 0), and equilibrium constant relation.)

subject: Mathematics
title: Trigonometry: Compound, Double & Multiple Angle Identities
formulaOrRule:
Compound Angle Addition Formulas: $\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B, \quad \cos(A \pm B) = \cos A \cos B \mp \sin A \sin B$;
Double Angle & Half Angle Formulas: $\sin 2A = 2\sin A \cos A, \quad \cos 2A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 A$

variablesOrTerms.B: Second angle in radians or degrees

derivationOrExplanation:
Derived from rotation coordinates on unit circle: cos(A - B) = x_A x_B + y_A y_B = cos A cos B + sin A sin B. Replacing B with -B yields sum formula. Applying complementary angle shifts π/2 - θ yields sin(A ± B).
Drill: Evaluate the exact value of sin(75°) by expanding sin(45° + 30°).

Substitute B = A into compound formulas: sin(A + A) = sin A cos A + cos A sin A = 2 sin A cos A. For cosine: cos(A + A) = cos A cos A - sin A sin A = cos²A - sin²A. Substituting sin²A = 1 - cos²A gives 2cos²A - 1.
Drill: If sin A = 3/5 with A in the first quadrant, calculate sin(2A) and cos(2A).

flashcard.front: What are the core equations and laws for Trigonometry: Compound, Double & Multiple Angle Identities?
flashcard.back:
$\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B, \quad \cos(A \pm B) = \cos A \cos B \mp \sin A \sin B$ (Fundamental angle sum and difference trigonometric identities.)
$\sin 2A = 2\sin A \cos A, \quad \cos 2A = \cos^2 A - \sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 A$ (Expressing double angles in terms of single angle products and powers.)

subject: Mathematics
title: Algebra & Coordinate Geometry: Binomial Theorem & Conic Sections
formulaOrRule:
Binomial Theorem & General Term: $(a + b)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n {^n C_r} a^{n-r} b^r, \quad T_{r+1} = {^n C_r} a^{n-r} b^r \quad \left[^n C_r = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}\right]$;
Standard Conic Sections (Parabola & Ellipse): $\text{Parabola: } y^2 = 4ax, \quad \text{Ellipse: } \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \quad (e = \sqrt{1 - b^2/a^2})$

variablesOrTerms.T_{r+1}: Value of the (r+1)-th term in binomial expansion
variablesOrTerms.b: Semi-minor axis of ellipse (b² = a²(1 - e²))
variablesOrTerms.e: Eccentricity (e = 1 for parabola, 0 < e < 1 for ellipse)
variablesOrTerms.4a: Latus rectum length of standard parabola

derivationOrExplanation:
The product (a + b) multiplied n times produces 2ⁿ terms. Choosing term b from r factors and a from remaining (n - r) factors can occur in ⁿCᵣ distinct combinations, yielding general term T_{r+1} = ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ.
Drill: Find the 5th term (T_5) in the binomial expansion of (2x - 3y)⁸.

Locus of point P whose distance from focus S equals eccentricity e times distance from directrix PM: SP = e · PM. For parabola e = 1 => (x - a)² + y² = (x + a)² => y² = 4ax. For ellipse e < 1 => x²/a² + y²/b² = 1.
Drill: For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/16 = 1, find the eccentricity e, coordinates of the foci, and length of latus rectum.

subject: Computer
title: Computer Science: Boolean Algebra & Algorithm Complexity

variablesOrTerms.B: Base memory address of array in RAM (bytes / hexadecimal)
variablesOrTerms.C: Total number of columns in array matrix
variablesOrTerms.W: Size of each element in bytes (e.g. 4 bytes for integer)

derivationOrExplanation:
Proven by exhaustive truth table evaluation across all 4 states of (A, B) ∈ {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)}. For (0,0): NOT(0+0) = 1 and NOT(0)·NOT(0) = 1. The principle of duality interchanges + and · and literals with their complements.
Drill: Simplify the boolean logic expression using De Morgan's laws: Y = NOT( (A · NOT(B)) + C ).

Binary search halves the search space at each comparison: remaining space after k steps is n / 2^k. Search terminates when n / 2^k <= 1 => 2^k >= n => k = ⌈log₂ n⌉. Maximum comparisons = floor(log₂ n) + 1.
Drill: A sorted array contains 1,000,000 records. What is the maximum number of comparisons needed to find an item using binary search?

In row-major order, rows are stored consecutively in 1D contiguous RAM. To reach row i, skip (i - L_r) full rows of C elements each. Within row i, skip (j - L_c) elements. Multiplying total elements skipped by word size W and adding base address B yields physical byte location.
Drill: An array A[10][20] is stored in row-major order starting at base address 2000 with 4 bytes per element. Find the address of A[4][7].

flashcard.front: What are the core equations and laws for Computer Science: Boolean Algebra & Algorithm Complexity?
flashcard.back:
$\overline{A + B} = \overline{A} \cdot \overline{B} \quad \text{and} \quad \overline{A \cdot B} = \overline{A} + \overline{B}$ (Complement of logical disjunction equals conjunction of complements, and vice versa.)
$O(1) < O(\log n) < O(n) < O(n\log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n), \quad C_{\text{binary search}} = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ (Strict order of algorithmic computational complexity growth and binary search comparison bound.)
$\text{Address}(A[i][j]) = B + W \times \left[(i - L_r) \times C + (j - L_c)\right]$ (Linear RAM byte address of an element A[i][j] in a 2D matrix stored in Row-Major order.)

formulaOrRule:
Celsius to Fahrenheit Scale Equivalence: $\frac{C}{5} = \frac{F - 32}{9} \quad \iff \quad F = \left(\frac{9}{5}C\right) + 32$;

variablesOrTerms.T: Time period of single oscillation (seconds, s)

variablesOrTerms.n: Number of full oscillation cycles counted (scalar)

A complete oscillation passes from mean position to both extremes and back. Total time t divided by cycle count n yields period T.
Drill: A pendulum takes 44 seconds to complete 20 full oscillations. Compute its period and frequency.

flashcard.front: What are the core equations and laws for Science: Temperature Scale Conversion & Simple Pendulums?
flashcard.back:

$T = \frac{t_{\text{total}}}{n} \quad \text{and} \quad f = \frac{1}{T}$ (Time period of one complete back-and-forth oscillation cycle.)

subject: Mathematics
title: Mathematics: Compound Interest & Cylinder Mensuration
formulaOrRule:
Compound Interest (Annual Compounding): $A = P\left(1 + \frac{R}{100}\right)^n \quad \text{and} \quad \text{CI} = A - P$;
Right Circular Cylinder Surface Area & Volume: $V = \pi r^2 h, \quad \text{CSA} = 2\pi rh, \quad \text{TSA} = 2\pi r(h + r)$

variablesOrTerms.TSA: Total surface area including top and bottom lids (m²)

derivationOrExplanation:
Year 1 amount is P(1+R/100). Year 2 amount is P(1+R/100)². By mathematical induction, period n gives A = P(1+R/100)ⁿ.
Drill: Compute compound interest on ₹10,000 for 2 years at 10% per annum compounded annually.

Unrolling curved surface yields a rectangle of length 2πr and height h, giving CSA = 2πrh. Adding two circular end discs gives TSA = 2πrh + 2πr².
Drill: A cylindrical tank has radius 7 m and height 10 m. Compute its CSA, TSA, and Volume.

flashcard.front: What are the core equations and laws for Mathematics: Compound Interest & Cylinder Mensuration?
flashcard.back:
$A = P\left(1 + \frac{R}{100}\right)^n \quad \text{and} \quad \text{CI} = A - P$ (Amount and compound interest when interest compounds annually over n conversion periods.)
$V = \pi r^2 h, \quad \text{CSA} = 2\pi rh, \quad \text{TSA} = 2\pi r(h + r)$ (Volume and lateral / total surface area of a closed right circular cylinder.)

subject: Science
title: Science: Pressure, Thrust and Acoustic Wave Speed
formulaOrRule:
Pressure and Thrust Equation: $P = \frac{F_{\perp}}{A} \quad \left(1\text{ Pa} = 1\text{ N/m}^2\right)$;
Acoustic Wave Speed Equation: $v = f \lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T}$

variablesOrTerms.v: Wave propagation speed (metres per second, m/s)
variablesOrTerms.\\lambda: Wavelength between consecutive wave crests / compressions (metres, m)
variablesOrTerms.T: Time period of one complete oscillation cycle (seconds, s)

derivationOrExplanation:
Pressure measures normal force concentration. Reducing contact area surcharges pressure for constant thrust.
Drill: A wooden block weighing 600 N rests on contact dimensions 0.5 m × 0.2 m. Calculate pressure in Pa.

Speed is distance divided by time. In one period T, wave advances distance λ: v = λ/T. Since f = 1/T, v = fλ.
Drill: A tuning fork vibrates at 512 Hz. In air with sound speed 340 m/s, find the sound wavelength.

flashcard.front: What are the core equations and laws for Science: Pressure, Thrust and Acoustic Wave Speed?
flashcard.back:
$P = \frac{F_{\perp}}{A} \quad \left(1\text{ Pa} = 1\text{ N/m}^2\right)$ (Normal compressive force concentrated per unit planar contact area.)
$v = f \lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T}$ (Relation connecting wave speed, vibrational frequency, and wavelength.)

subject: Physics
title: Physics: Moment of Force (Torque) & Fluid Pressure
formulaOrRule:
Moment of Force (Torque) & Principle of Moments: $\tau = F \times d_{\perp} \quad \text{and} \quad \sum \tau_{\text{anticlockwise}} = \sum \tau_{\text{clockwise}}$;
Hydrostatic Liquid Pressure: $P = h \rho g$

variablesOrTerms.d_perp: Perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action of force (metres, m)

derivationOrExplanation:
Turning efficacy scales with both force magnitude and lever arm length: τ = F × d. For equilibrium, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.
Drill: A mechanic applies 75 N force at the end of a 0.24 m spanner. Find the torque generated in N·m.

Weight of liquid column is W = m·g = (A·h·ρ)·g. Dividing by base area A gives P = W/A = hρg.
Drill: Find hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of a 15 m lake filled with water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²).

flashcard.front: What are the core equations and laws for Physics: Moment of Force (Torque) & Fluid Pressure?
flashcard.back:
$\tau = F \times d_{\perp} \quad \text{and} \quad \sum \tau_{\text{anticlockwise}} = \sum \tau_{\text{clockwise}}$ (Rotational turning effect of force about a pivot axis and rotational equilibrium law.)
$P = h \rho g$ (Pressure exerted by a static liquid column at vertical depth h.)
